speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise today with pride to report to the House of Commons the progress of the XV Olympic Winter Games in Calgary as well as a review of the preparations which led to making these games the most successful winter games in the history of the Olympic movement.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext:
To begin with, the success rests with the fact that from the very beginning there was a partnership formed, a partnership between the federal Government, the provincial Government of Alberta and the City of Calgary, very much along with the private and corporate sector from coast to coast, all under the terrific direction of the organizing committee known as OCO '88. This partnership led toward preparing and developing the best facilities, the best organizations and the best infrastructure that any games have ever seen.
The commitment on the part of the Government of Canada was $200 million in non-tax revenue dollars, and I want to make that very clear. We have been able to raise those non-tax dollars from such events as the sale of commemorative Olympic coins world wide, an agreement with provincial lottery organizations, the obtaining of the seignorage from the circulating dollar coin and so on.
The biggest aspect of raising these funds is the sale of the Olympic commemorative coins. As a result of the tremendous respect of the Royal Canadian Mint, we are selling those coins in Japan, in the United States, in western Europe and all over the world. We are bringing those currencies into Canada to build facilities in Calgary, not only for these games but for the use by Canadians for generations to come. We are proud that we have been able to contribute as a federal Government toward the success of these games without costing the taxpayer one red cent. We have contributed toward the success of the games, but beyond that, as well we have contributed toward making a legacy which will go on for generations, leaving an economic benefit which began even before the games began.
Very briefly, before the opening ceremonies took place on February 13, the economic benefits of the preparation of the Calgary Olympics was an influx of new dollars, $1.3 billion, into the Gross Domestic Product of Canada. This not only affects Calgary and Alberta but the whole country, because

February 22, 1988
Statements by Ministers
obviously when preparing for the games one must provide services and products from coast to coast. Even before the games began, there was a benefit of $1.3 billion and the creation of some 27,000 person-years of employment. These facilities, which were constructed on time and under budget, are the best state-of-the-art technology facilities ever to be constructed anywhere in the world. They will be used after the games, not only by high performance athletes from Canada and around the world, but by the public at large because this is a people-oriented Olympics.
In fact, I believe that the success of the federal Government's involvement in the preparation of these Olympics was best summed up by the Auditor General, who very seldom has praise for anything, who in his most recent report concluded that the federal Government's financial management of its involvement in the Olympic Games was, in an unprecedented manner, well managed. In fact, he suggested that it was done in a brilliant fashion and that all Canadians can be proud of the accomplishment of the Government and the people of Canada in preparing the facilities for the games.
In addition to the federal Government's contribution of $125 million to the facilities it contributed another $45 million toward the organization of the games, also non-tax revenues, and most important, and for the first time, we have established from non-tax revenue sources a $30 million endowment fund. The proceeds of the endowment fund will be used to operate these facilities in the future so that there will be no burden on the taxpayer to operate those facilities after the games.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, that describes the preparation of the facilities and the games themselves. 1 have had the opportunity as a Canadian to participate in the Olympics, both as an athlete and as a television commentator for many years. One of the things which I felt was wrong in previous Olympics in other countries was that the spirit of the games was restricted to the host city. I felt it was very important to try to spread the Olympic spirit to every community across Canada.
When I presented that proposal to Cabinet it was unanimously supported and we came up with the Celebration '88 program in which Members from all sides of the House have participated with much enthusiasm. Celebration '88 leading up to the games gave every Canadian the opportunity to participate in some way, shape, or form in the Olympic spirit within their own communities. We developed an educational package for our youth which all the provinces distributed to the elementary schools. We developed with the communities at the community level special Olympic community events.
Most important of all, I suppose, are the ceremonies to recognize those people in every community who contributed in their way, be it as a coach, a sponsor, an athlete, a volunteer, or an official. This has given all of us in the House of Commons an opportunity to recognize individuals within our own
communities for the contributions they have made to sport and to the community based on the Olympic program.
The heart and soul of this program, of course, was the torch relay. 1 need not remind Members of the tremendous emotion which came from the hearts as Canadians came out on the streets to watch the torch go through their communities. I do not believe that in my lifetime 1 have seen such emotion pour out of Canadians from every walk of life as it did during the torch relay. That emotion, of course, has been carried into Calgary for the games. There is no doubt in my mind that the Celebration '88 program with the torch relay produced perhaps the most unifying effect that this country has seen in decades, if ever.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext:
So the torch moved to Calgary on February 13 for the beginning of 16 days of celebrations that will live on in this country forever. It is not only 16 days of celebration of sport, Mr. Speaker, it is 16 days of celebration of culture, a celebration of the arts, a celebration of youth coming together from all parts of the world in harmony and in peace, all in the spirit of the Olympic movement. That is what the games are all about.
1 can say, as a former athlete and, more important, as a Canadian, that when the Canadian team walked into McMahon Stadium on February 13 my chest swelled out and my heart pumped a little faster. The pride and emotion of the
60,000	people in that stadium and the 1.5 billion people watching Canada through the eyes of television put Canada right on top of the heap worldwide and brought something into Canadian hearts and minds which was long in coming.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext:
When young Robyn Perry, the 11-year old Calgarian figure skater, ran up the steps to light the cauldron it was beyond words. That young Canadian was the symbol of the youth of the world, symbolizing what the Olympic spirit means, not only to sport and not only to Canadians but to the youth of the world.
The games began with a people-oriented event and as we approach the last few days of the Olympics we see that it is indeed a people-oriented Olympics. More tickets have been sold and more people have participated than in any previous Olympics. In fact, ticket sales have zoomed to well over 1.5 million. The highest level of sales prior to these Olympics was in Sarajevo, Yugoslavia, four years ago when 435,000 tickets were sold. In Calgary over 1.5 million tickets have been sold and the events are jam-packed. The medal ceremonies every night in the downtown plaza attract an average of 50,000 people. The 70-metre ski jump was watched by over 70,000 people. The enthusiasm has spread to every corner of Calgary and is spreading to every corner of Canada and the world as well.
February 22, 1988

I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate, on behalf of the Government of Canada and on behalf of Parliament, not only the organizers of the games but the thousands and thousands of volunteers who made this people-Olympics a reality. The volunteers come from every walk of life. The other day 1 was driven in a car by a volunteer who is a company executive whose salary is probably $250,000 a year. Yet, for the duration of a month, he volunteered his time and services to make the Olympics a success. Calgarians and Canadians have opened up their homes and their hearts to the world. We have shown the world that we can compete. We have shown the world the warmth, hospitality, enthusiasm, friendship, and generosity that Canadians are all about. Right now the world is envious of this tremendous success.
Finally, none of this could happen without the athletes. Our athletes have contributed so much of themselves in their young lifetimes. I speak as a former Olympian and I know that you give up all of your normal life as you prepare to represent, not only yourself-that is secondary-but your family, your community and, most of all, your country. The greatest Olympian Canada has ever had is Gaetan Boucher with his tremendous courage. We are so proud of him.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext:
The spirit of Brian Orser and the determination of Karen Percy symbolize the Canadian athletes' commitment and spirit to compete on behalf of themselves and Canada. We are all very proud of their achievement and efforts.
Perhaps this is a little bit out of line with what we should or should not do in this place, but if 1 may through you, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to convey also our thanks and congratulations to the parents of these athletes. They have made it possible for them to give of their lives to the sport, to Canada, and to the Olympic movement. You happen to be one of those parents, Mr. Speaker, and we were very proud yesterday when your daughter, Anna Fraser, represented Canada so dramatically in the aerials in free style skiing.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext:
We thank you for your efforts and I hope, sir, that through you we are able to pass our thanks and congratulations to all the parents of our Canadian athletes who are making us so proud.
I wish it had been my idea to come forward with the parents program that Labatt's, one of the official sponsors of the Olympic Games, initiated in order to bring the families and the parents of our Olympic athletes to Calgary. Labatt's, as well as all the sponsors associated with the Olympic games in Calgary should be congratulated.
If 1 sound a little emotional and a little over enthusiastic, it is because I am. I come from a country where many of our
Statements by Ministers
freedoms were taken away. My parents had the wisdom to choose this country which gives Canadians hopes and aspirations, opportunities and freedoms that no other country can match. It is because of these opportunities, because of these freedoms, because of these hopes and aspirations that we can share with the rest of the world the tremendous accomplishments that Canadians have brought to themselves, to Canada and the Olympic movement.
The spirit of the Olympics is the desire of mankind to come together in friendship and harmony in order to bring peace and a better understanding to all parts of the world. The Olympics is far more than just a bunch of skiers going down a ski slope, or a bunch of skaters skating in circles. It is through this Olympic spirit that we can make the world a better place, not just for ourselves but for our children and grandchildren.
The Calgary Olympics have contributed toward that goal. We as Canadians can be very proud of this tremendous accomplishment on behalf of peace and freedom everywhere around the world through the eyes of the Olympic Games.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON PREPARATIONS AND PROGRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I voice on behalf of the Official Opposition our congratulations and continued support to Canada's athletes participating in the XV Winter Olympics now being held in Calgary.

Mr. Speaker, it was Baron Pierre de Coubertin who in 1896 brought the world a proposal for restoring the Olympiads of Ancient Greece. As we all know, the first Winter Olympics were held in Chamonix, France, in 1924. At the time, the Winter Games were only a kind of mini-Olympics, but today, the Winter Games have achieved the same status as the Summer Olympics.

Mr. Gordon Douglas, a legislative assistant to one of my colleagues, was in France last week. He told me that he had the opportunity to see the Calgary Olympics through the eyes of the world and that the coverage and prestige of the Olympics was extensive and a compliment to us as a nation.
Half-way through the international games, all Canadians can be proud of the dedication, determination and sportsmanship exhibited by our athletes in competing against the world's best. The outstanding Silver Medal figure skating performance of Brian Orser of Penatanguishene, Ontario, was breathtaking to watch. The Bronze Medal downhill run of Banffs Karen Percy was equally breathtaking and the tens of thousands who turned out for the awards ceremony last Friday is a reflection of Canada's pride in her performance.
Mr. Speaker, occasionally I try to ski and, while I enjoy it, I do not do a very good job. I had very special admiration while watching a famous skier you know very well, your daughter

Canada's men and women curling teams won medals in their demonstration sport. The Gold Medal to the women's team and the Bronze Medal won by the men's team reflect Canada's continuing international domination of this very popular sport.
I want to speak briefly about the Best Ever fund, some $25 million that was injected toward assisting our athletes. Today I read a newspaper article which indicated that the funding had not been a success because, in the opinion of the writer, the results were not as they should have been. I want to respectfully disagree with that. 1 suggest that just keeping up with the other countries that are ever improving their own athletes-we have certainly kept up so far, with the best days yet to come- is a tangible measure that the Best Ever fund had and hopefully will continue to have in the future.

Mr. Speaker, in 1976 I had the privilege of being one of the bearers of the Olympic Flame. 1 carried the torch between Ontario and Quebec, at Cumberland, Ontario, when the Torch crossed the river into our neighbouring province. For me it was a very special privilege, as a Quebecer by birth and a Franco-Ontarian by adoption, to provide the link between the two provinces by carrying the Olympic Torch.
This year, like everybody else I put my name in for the draw for bearers of the Olumpic Torch, but I was not as lucky as in 1976. I can't say 1 lacked political pull, but I didn't have the luck of the draw, Mr. Speaker.
1 was lucky just the same, because the Olympic Torch stopped in my riding in Casselman, Ontario, and I want to thank the officials and directors of Petro-Canada for making it possible for my riding to take part in the Olympic Torch relay.
I would like to say a few words about Celebration '88. The Minister said earlier that many Members took advantage of this event to involve their communities in the program. 1 am one of those Members. In my case, Mr. Speaker, fifteen municipalities in my riding participated. I personally met with municipal authorities, and during the holidays, my senior assistant, Andre Tessier, met with all municipalities to encourage as many as possible to participate. In fact, especially thanks to the excellent work done by my assistant, a lot of these municipalities did in fact participate.
Saturday evening I was visiting the municipality of Planta-genet South, a very small one in my riding, where I had the
privilege, on behalf of the Government and on behalf of our country, of giving six Celebration '88 medals to local volunteers.
Mr. Speaker, volunteers have worked in our communities for decades. Today, thanks to Celebration '88, we have a way of expressing our recognition for the major contribution they have made. I therefore would like to congratulate the people who initiated the Celebration '88 Program, and if the Minister himself is responsible, 1 want him to accept my congratulations. If it was one of his officials, I hope he will transmit my congratulations to the person concerned, because Celebration '88 is an excellent program and one that was long overdue.
In addition to medals, Celebration '88 also gives Members a chance to hand out merit certificates. These are signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Member concerned. I have handed out about nearly 300 certificates in my own riding, Mr. Speaker, the names of the recipients being provided by the various municipalities. 1 must say it does not happen very often that my name and the Prime Minister's appear on the same document. When we realize 300 of these certificates have been handed out in my riding, it becomes an exceptional performance indeed. I want to congratulate the Minister on this initiative as well, because there are certainly more than six individuals per municipality who deserve recognition. So for the others, we have the certificates, which probably did not cost that much to make, but which are nevertheless a token of appreciation, by the various governments, of the work done by all these volunteers and all those who have been working for years to help their communities.
The Calgary Winter Olympic Games would not be the international success that they are without the hard work of the thousands of volunteers who have assisted. The Minister enumerated cases of individuals who have given up so much of their time. He has referred to company executives, for example, who took their time to participate as volunteers in the Olympics. Many individuals who participated as volunteers probably had to make tremendous sacrifices to do so. Some of them used hard-earned dollars that they could have used for themselves, but instead they chose to spend their own money in order to assist others and to participate in the Olympic movement. Those people deserve our congratulations indeed.
These men and women also deserve our congratulations for ensuring that the Calgary Winter Olympic Games are a meeting place of nations in friendly competition. They are indeed, as the Minister has said, the best Olympic games yet.

Mr. Speaker, I was Opposition critic at the time Parliament passed the Bill authorizing the Royal Canadian Mint to manufacture the Olympic Coin. I am proud that our Party supported this initiative, and I am delighted to see how successful this program has been.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Olympics is a dream, a dream come true for the young athletes who are participating in the games. It is a dream come true for the world in that we are able to carry out an international activity in a co-operative spirit, and a dream come true for Canadians. We are hosts to the world and to the best in the world.

Today, we are proud to be Canadians.

We are proud to be Canadians.
1 want to mention three things about the Olympics. 1 want to talk a bit about the athletes and about the politics of the Olympics and I want to say a few words about Olympic journalism.
To one who has only recently adopted the practice of exercise, in fact in the last few weeks, the Olympics is an Everest that requires super human dedication, commitment and capacity to mount. I am inspired by the young people who are participating in the Olympics and by the young Canadians who are at the Olympic games. To be at the Olympics, simply to be there and to be a part of the games, is an attainment, the fulfilment of a dream. It is the culmination of a long process of dedication and of sacrifice by athletes and by their families. To be at the Olympics, whether one wins a medal, places high or low-simply to be there-is a world class attainment.
We have much to learn from these young people about setting goals of excellence and about attainment. Yet we also have winners. There are those who find themselves in the winner's circle. Karen Percy was our first medal winner. She broke through to make Canada a winner. Brian Orser performed at the absolute epitome of athletic excellence. Many others including Linda Moore, Penny Ryan, Debbie Jones, Lindsay Sparkes, Ed Lukowich, John Ferguson, Neil Houston and Brent Syme are participating. Canada and its athletes are in the winner's circle.
I want to say a bit about the politics of the Olympics. 1 heard the Minister say that the Olympics would not cost the taxpayers one red cent. Of course, as a taxpayer 1 am glad that no additional burden will be put on my shoulders, but I do hope that this does not mean that the Government is blind to a few other lessons that are to be learned from this.
Statements by Ministers
In this Olympics there has been an appeal for private dollars. I must say that that is a good policy, but experience has shown that this works with popular sports like skiing. However, what about the less well known sports, the sports which are yet to gain a popular following? Is there not here a role for public dollars? What about the long-term development that is needed in order to lay the base for Olympic performance? Who will pay for the facilities and the coaching when the camera lights are no longer shining upon the arena? I hope the Government is not blind to the fact that there is a role for public dollars and that there is a long-term developmental process that must be supported. 1 hope the Government will see this rather than simply be restricted by some sort of ideological blinders.
Another aspect of the politics of the Olympics has to do with the Lubicon Indians. I hope that when the television cameras have left Calgary the Lubicon will be remembered. As native people, we have a dream too. We have a dream of justice. We have a dream of being treated fairly. When the cameras are gone from Calgary the Lubicon must be remembered, and the federal Government and the provincial Government must act to resolve that injustice. The federal Government and the provincial Governments must act to resolve that injustice.
1 have another perspective on the Olympics which I want to share with Hon. Members. It is with respect to Olympic journalism. I have been surprised, shocked and hurt by some of the reporting I have seen concerning the Olympics. I have seen what I would call political reporting being transferred to the covering of the games. It is fair ball to savage the Government and to ask loaded questions before TV cameras of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It is all right to perform a hatchet job on Ed Broadbent, Brian Mulroney, John Crosbie or John Turner. I want to say that when it comes to our young athletes, they should be left alone.
I find it incredible when I see in the paper a picture of Karen Percy, who broke through at the Olympics to make Canada a winner, with a reporter saying, "She didn't win a second medal". What kind of reporting is that? Brian Orser performed at world peak, yet a reporter came up to him with the cameras on and said, "We have good news and bad news for you. The good news is that you won a medal. The bad news is that you came in second. What do you have to say?" That may be all right for the battleground of politics, but it is one shabby way to treat our Olympic athletes.
Gaetan Boucher is world reknowned for his achievements. What did the media do to him? They put his picture on the front pages and wrote, "How come he only came in ninth?" The man had enormous courage to compete, in light of the record that he has behind him. He had the courage to put his world record at risk. I say to members of the media, clean up your journalism. If you want to be rough and tough and ask loaded questions, stay in the political arena but leave the athletes alone. This is a celebration of excellence. It is a

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition signed by a number of Canadians who indicate that the Conservative Government has no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised. They point out that the trade agreement negotiated by the Mulroney Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interest of Canadians, and to equalize opportunities between regions.
They state that the trade agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States. The proposed trade agreement not only denies Canadians secure access to the U.S. market, which was the key objective in these negotiations, but threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs.
Therefore the undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed Mulroney trade agreement during a national general election.

subsubtopic: SAFE CONTAINER FOR TRANSPORT OF PLUTONIUM
speechtext:
1.	Has the government, or an agency thereof, developed standards or criteria for a safe container in which to transport plutonium in an airplane and, if so, what are they?
2.	If such standards do not exist, are they being developed and, if so, (i) by whom (ii) when will they be ready?
3.	Will standards or criteria be adopted from other jurisdictions and if so, from which jurisdiction(s)?
4.	What are the specifics of the standards or criteria under consideration for adoption?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SAFE CONTAINER FOR TRANSPORT OF PLUTONIUM
speechtext:
The Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows:
1. and 2. Yes, there are standards and criteria for the safe containment, during transportation, of radioactive materials including plutonium. These are minimum regulatory safety standards for all radioactive materials and can be augmented by other limitations, terms and conditions, depending upon the specifics of a proposed shipment.
Under the Atomic Energy Control Act, the AECB is empowered to regulate the transportation of "prescribed substances", which include radioactive materials like plutonium.
The Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act also applies to all handling, offering for transport and transporting of "dangerous goods", by any means of transport. The AECB and Transport Canada jointly administer the regulation of the shipment of dangerous goods, like plutonium, through an Inter-Departmental Memorandum of Agreement on the Transport of Radioactive Materials.
The AECB administers the Transport Packaging of Radioactive Materials Regulations. These regulations establish the standards and criteria for the certification of packaging designed to contain plutonium for transport by any means of transport, including air. In any examination of the ability of a proposed container to meet the packaging performance standards of the regulations, the AECB is also empowered to consider any health, safety or security concern and to impose other limitations, terms and conditions on the use or the transportation of a package containing radioactive "prescribed substances".
Copies of the regulations are available, upon request, from the Radiosotopes and Tranportation Division, Atomic Energy Control Board, 270 Albert Street, Ottawa.
3. The above standards and criteria are based on those which have been developed by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Canada, as a founding member state, participates in the work of the IAEA in the continuous evaluation and development of criteria and standards dealing with the safe transport of radioactive material. At present, the IAEA is examining proposals dealing with shipments involving high consequence/low probability accidents; these proposals
The Budget-Mr. Charest
apply to shipments of radioactive materials, such as plutonium shipments by air and other means of transport.
4. There are no other standards or criteria, specific to plutonium, which are under consideration for adoption. However, there is a revision to some of the IAEA standards affecting radioactive materials. This revision has not yet been adopted internationally and the AECB is presently examining them for incorporation into Canadian legislation.

speechtext:
To clarify the matter, Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Bourassa is right in pointing out that when I ... To put an end to that, Mr. Speaker, I have no wish to burden you with that clarification. Since it was I who said it, I have no intention of implying in any way that the Hon. Member for Bourassa agrees with my speech, or perhaps part of it. He will have an opportunity to ask questions and make comments, if he so wishes, that is his choice.
Finally, to return to where we were in 1984, there were references to changes. Let us recall the context then, and in the main it is still the context that is prevailing today.
In 1984, Mr. Speaker, the world around us witnessed many changes. I think we must first list those changes. The global economic axis was changing, moving from the Atlantic to the Pacific and this is one reality that had to be addressed in 1984. Then we had the increasing importance of the service sector in the global economy, representing as it does some 25 per cent of the global GNP, which is reflected in Canada in that, among others, 75 per cent of jobs in this country are currently in the service sector. This is quite a radical development, considering especially that in 1945, Mr. Speaker, only some 40 per cent of jobs in Canada were in the area of services, as compared to 75 per cent in 1986. So already in 1984 that was quite a radical change.
The Budget-Mr. Charest
In addition, there was the emergence of the newly industrialized nations. I am referring here to Brazil which, by way of an aside, is going through quite a dramatic period, but which anyway can be characterized or labelled as one of the emerging nations among developing ones. South Korea is another example, Mr. Speaker, of industrializing nations. There is also Japan's current importance as one of our markets.
Among those new realities, there was also the relative decline of the United States, because other industrialized nations were emerging and the American trade deficit was whipping up protectionist trends in the United States. And this is a reality that is of very close significance to us Canadians, because some 80 per cent of our two-way trade, meaning both exports and imports, are with the United States. So this is of some significance to us as a nation.
One thing is clear in all this, and 1 believe that everyone can agree, namely that we could not accept the status quo. There had to be a change, and this change had to be rather comprehensive. What we have accomplished during the last three years is quite noteworthy. I am certain that Members on the other side will tell us that they do not agree with such or such an initiative, but no one can deny the fact that this Government has made a number of very important structural changes.
Among other things, this Government has provided Canada with a new trade policy. This is the first time such a thing has happened since 1879, when Sir John A. Macdonald developed in this House what was then called the national policy. It is the first time since 1879 that the Canadian Government has attempted to develop a comprehensive trade policy on two fronts, first by pursuing our interests within GATT, and second by deciding to negotiate a free trade agreement with our neighbours to the South, the Americans, to try to provide some stability in our trading relations with the United States as they account for 80 per cent of all our exports.
This is a basic change for Canada. We also established a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology, recognizing the need for Canada to acquire, develop and apply new industrial technologies if we want to remain competitive, while keeping in mind the fact that Canada is an exporting country, even though other countries are more dependent on their exports for their Gross National Product. Everyone agrees on this point, including the Liberals, the NPD and ourselves. We all agree that we are an exporting country and want to remain an exporting country. We do not necessarily agree on the means to do so, but we do agree on the basic facts.
I therefore assume that we also agree on the industrial consequence of such a choice, this consequence being that we have to acquire and apply new technologies. This is why this new Department was created.
Canada being made up of regions, we also developed new regional economic development policies based in large part on

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Charest
the principle that the local people are always in the best position to manage their own economy and make their own decisions. This is why the federal Government decentralized its administrative machinery to manage its regional economic development programs. This was done in Western Canada. It was also done in Eastern Canada, in the Atlantic region. It was also done for Northern Ontario. We re-established the Laprade Fund in Quebec, and there is also the Eastern Plan.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a country made up of regions, and so these very tangible and very real instruments have been made available to enable the regions to implement better management standards and look after their own administration.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, people are wont to forget a basic fact, namely that this Government has been sponsoring a new employment policy. The employment planning strategy was the result of the First Ministers' Conference held in Regina in 1985, a historic conference where the federal Government, the provinces, the private sector, labour unions and a host of interest groups in our society co-operated and reached a consensus on a new employment planning strategy geared to our country's current priorities.
We have three major priorities. First we concluded that from here on in we had to emphasize training under our employment programs, that it was no longer good enough to sponsor job programs only to keep people busy, that we had to take a further step and do more for these people by making training facilities available to them in an attempt to determine whether they would be employable. We wanted these people to look forward to regular work instead of going from job programs to unemployment benefits or yet other work programs.
Mr. Speaker, the second priority of the employment planning strategy was to concentrate on people who had been out of work for twenty weeks or more, because it stands to reason that they are the ones who find it more difficult to rejoin the labour force.
And, thirdly, Mr. Speaker, under the employment planning strategy, we have also sought other partners, because jobs creation should not be the concern of only one government in Canada, nor that of only one industry, but it should be the concern of all those involved, namely the private sector, the unions, the non-profit and public organizations at every level, whether municipal or provincial. That is why we wanted to include as many partners as possible.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, people have a tendency to forget that this Government has also administered this country along principles which are our own as Progressive Conservatives; hence our deregulation, privitization, tax reform and deficit control policies. That is a management strategy which properly reflects the philosophy of our party, a philosophy which we had clearly enunciated in 1984. Having received the full support of Canadian voters during the 1984 election, we performed exactly as we had promised.
In our opinion, it was important to administer the country along these principles for the following reason: In view of foreign factors which influence us and cannot be denied, as evidenced by the recent stock exchange crash.
Clearly, nobody can deny that events occurring outside of Canada have a serious impact on us. If Canada wants to meet head-on the new challenges confronting us, and occupy the place it deserves, if we want to solve the new problems, the Govenment's organization must be flexible enough to meet these needs. More than ever before, Mr. Speaker, people involved in business or trade unions at every level should develop the necessary flexibility to meet as quickly and efficiently as possible the challenges confronting us, which is not easy. The only way to do it as the Federal Government, on the basis of our Progressive Conservative philosophy, is to try to lighten the Government machinery to make it as flexible as possible. Some people will say to us: Well, the Government is opting out. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with such a conclusion. If the Government was in fact opting out, why did we produce, for instance, a national policy on child care? Is that the way a government willing to opt or back out behaves? Not at all, quite the contrary! My goodness, it seems to me an initiative as important as this one is evidence of a government's dedication to its citizens and its intention to make its presence felt. But instead of being inhibiting, of being an obstacle, that presence should rather facilitate change and allow to manage it better, and on a personal basis, leave individuals free to decide on their own without trying to guide them in their choices or impose choices on them.
Beyond all that, Mr Speaker, as a country, if we wanted to meet those challenges, we had to be able to prepare better for the great changes we are going through; we also had to bring reconciliation within Canada. It is with some joy, I think, that all Members of this House witnessed the signing of the Meech Lake Accord, debated it here, and were finally able to recognize the significance of the national reconciliation which we owe in part if not totally, I must say, to the efforts of the Prime Minister. It will no doubt remain one of his most magnificent achievements.
What is the purpose of all this? That question must be asked. We did all that. In 1984, we promised change-external factors are urging us on, we produced for Canada new policies on trade, investment, regional economic development, and employment. We achieved national reconciliation. But what was our goal? I think it is becoming clear that, for this Government, what we want for Canada is a new role in the world. What we are trying to do is redefine Canada's international role. We wish to achieve this objective in a context where Americans and superpowers generally are less powerful-not because they get poorer in absolute terms but because other countries get richer. Such a new balance would provide Canada, as a country, with an absolutely outstanding opportunity.
It would mean a stronger position for us to influence world affairs so that they reflect increasingly our Canadian values.
February 22, 1988

There are concrete examples of that. That will and those hopes and wishes have made it possible for us to hold the Sommet de la Francophonie. It is the Canadian Government and our Prime Minister who made that summit possible and the leadership role we have in that regard is by no means an accident. It is no accident either that Canada, which is a North American country, plays a leadership role in the Commonwealth. And it is no accident that we signed a free-trade deal with the U.S. while pursuing our leadership role within GATT. It is no accident, Mr. Speaker, that Canada and this Government have a new national defence policy that recognizes our commitment to NATO while emphasizing Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic. And it will be a great moment in our history when the Prime Minister welcomes the leaders of the Group of Seven nations next June in Toronto, which is now said to be a "world city"? At last, they got the same status as Montreal, if I may be more provincial in my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the fact that Canada plays a more important part in the world, and there is a reason for all that. Our underlying motivation is the following: as a Government and as a country on the everchanging world scene which gives us an opportunity to play a more significant part, we want to promote our own values, our own views about the environment for example, our great traditions of tolerance, social peace within our community, of justice and equity. In conclusion all this reflects how Canadians behave in their everyday lives: their stand on multiculturalism and bilingualism. This is part of our country, this is what Canada and Canadian men and women are all about. And by occupying a greater place in the world, with a little luck and a little conceit too, admittedly, we hope to make the world where we live in closer to our own image.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest). The Minister made reference to the positive program as far as child care is concerned that his Government promised. Indeed, there have been promises over three years, perhaps four, that there would be major action taken regarding the very urgent crisis in Canada and the need for many more licensed quality child care spaces for our children, particularly those of working parents. Yet in this Budget to which the Minister is supposedly speaking he really has not acknowledged that. Aside from doubling a very regressive tax measure, there is nothing in the Budget to show the Government's commitment to increased funding for child care spaces. This is a very desperate need.
Would the Minister explain and clarify that? His statement did not give the real picture. Why is there nothing in the Budget to begin making some impact on the child care crisis in Canada? I am talking about increased licensed quality spaces, with a decent rate of pay for care givers and affordable fees for children across the country?

speechtext: The period for questions and comments is over. Debate. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to put on record some thoughts
February 22, 1988

with regard to this Budget and the Government. The Government promised fairness, honesty, and equity to Canadians and has not delivered. As many of the media commentators have said, this is not so much a Budget as an attempt by the Government to change the agenda of the country which has been unfortunately so absorbed with the many scandals and failures of the Government. It is attempting to convince Canadians that it is really not all bad and to praise itself in a pre-election period.
We are very disappointed, as I am sure most Canadians who have studied this Budget are, about the lost opportunities which have been epitomized in this Budget. The Budget will do nothing for average Canadians. In fact, it contains some regressive measures for them including an increased tax on gas which could cost families about $50 a year extra. In particular, it does nothing to try to deal with the very serious problems which still exist in ridings such as my riding of Vancouver East where there continues to be a very high incidence of poverty and a very high rate of unemployment.
We believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had a real opportunity to move to greater regional fairness, to stop the rise in interest rates which is a very major factor in our economic growth and development, and to make the tax system fairer, which is something the Government has been promising us over and over again. However, there is no attention paid to these things in this Budget.
The Minister also promised to implement the national child care program which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) have been promising for years. If 1 sounded very angry when asking questions of the previous speaker, it is because 1 was angry. It is all very well to talk about promises which have been made as if they have been fulfilled. However, there is no child care for most families across the country right now. Nothing has been put forward in this Budget to help to increase the number of licensed quality child care spaces.
The Member can talk at great length about promises, but that does nothing for families with young children who have needed and been promised child care facilities for a number of years and will now obviously have to wait until after an election. This sounds to me like a lot of election propaganda again. Therefore, the Budget is very unfair.
One of the things about which we are particularly concerned is that it is really building two Canadas. You will recall that the Prime Minister warned us a year ago that "we are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is under-developed and underemployed". Speaking of one who comes from an underdeveloped and under-employed region of Canada, and certainly from a constituency which has a high rate of unemployment, I could not agree more. I am very disappointed that during the Minister's last period in office-because he is on his way out, as is the Government-he has done nothing to try to fulfil promises of regional fairness.
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
The Budget ignores the fact that unemployment in British Columbia, in seven other provinces, and in the North is still at the level which prevailed during the 1981, 1982, and 1983 recessions. Through one of the job development projects we recently did a study in my riding of Vancouver East. 1 sent the study to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). That study showed that in Vancouver East 27.5 per cent of those actively seeking work cannot find jobs. Not all of those statistics show up at the unemployment office, but that is the real rate of unemployment. That is an intolerable situation. I happened to mention that to a colleague of mine from a northern riding who said that there are communities in his riding within which the unemployment rate is over 50 per cent, particularly native communities.
We should have a policy of full employment. We should have a Government which will make this a top priority rather than only talking about how unemployment has gone down in central Canada. We should be working on full employment across the country. This Budget and the trade deal with the United States will not assist in this kind of equality.
The Government had an opportunity to correct unfairness in the tax reform Budget of last year but did nothing. The result is that the average Canadian family will be paying more than $1,000 in additional taxes than in 1984. I stress "families" because families are being penalized more than are those who do not have children. Only the richest 2 per cent of taxpayers will pay less. As a further consequence of this Budget, 60,000 corporations will continue to pay no tax. That group could have been paying taxes to provide revenue for the programs which are necessary, including a much more generous program for child care.
Nothing was done to reduce the interest rate levels which we think would help considerably to develop economic diversification and deal with unemployment. Canadians were looking for fairness but nothing is offered in this Budget to close the growing disparity between people in central Canada and in Canada's East, West, and North, and the disparities between rich and poor which will remain indeed they are increasing. I will expand on that a little later.
Are these the policies of fairness which the Government promised? If they are, the voters and citizens of Canada are sorely disappointed.
I would like to refer very briefly to a couple of analyses of the Budget which show that the rich have won control over Canada's tax system. I will not go into this in detail.
The Institute for Research on Public Policy said that the richest people in the country are the big winners, no matter how you slice it. They went on to say that 1988 personal income tax reform will increase the disposable income of Canadian taxpayers, with the biggest gainers in the top one per cent, but leaves the majority worse off than in 1984.

February 22. 1988
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
Linda McQuaig did an analysis in her book entitled Behind Closed Doors. She looked at the total Conservative approach to tax reform and concluded, again, that the tax system keeps moving away from the ideals of fairness and equity and that, in fact, the system has created measures where the poor and middle class keep paying more tax while the rich end up paying less.
As critic for social policy, I want to focus on aspects of the Budget that have an impact on families. Average families have already suffered under the economic policies of the Government, particularly as they relate to tax measures. They have seen a considerable loss in family benefits, which 1 will explain in detail later.
They are still paying high taxes and have been hit hardest by the sales tax. Families raising children must buy many more consumer goods and spend most of their money for essentials. The sales tax hits family consumers much more than single or higher income people.
The Canadian Council on Social Development has made some profound statements based on their analysis and the analysis of the National Council of Welfare. They state:
One segment of the Canadian population which has not advanced during this government's term is families with dependent children . . . Families with children have lost ground compared with other Canadian households. The effects of partially deindexing all family benefit programs and tax credits in conjunction with tax reform measures will mean that a one-earner couple with two kids and an income of $30,000 will pay $1,439 more in total income and federal consumption taxes in 1990 than in 1984, after adjusting for inflation.
This is compared to a similar couple with no kids who will pay $979 more. What kind of equity is that?
The CCSD also stated that minimum wage workers under federal jurisdiction have fared particularly badly. This includes the working poor group who have lost about one-third of their income to inflation since 1980. The CCSD went on to say:
The 50 per cent increase in 1986 prevented the situation from deteriorating further but the federal minimum wage rate still rates second from the bottom compared with all provincial rates.
They go on to summarize:
Major new measures were not announced in the Budget. But continued deindexation hits families with children much harder than it affects adults without children. This is a most regressive way to raise revenue for deficit reduction.
The Budget also announced continued reductions in non statutory programs, amounting to $300 million. There is very little detail in the Budget Papers about what programs will be affected by this Budget reduction measure. Non statutory programs include very many small but important programs such as social housing programs, training programs, programs for women, as well as family support programs.
As pointed out by the CCSD, the benefits for a family of four have decreased and are about $300 less for low income families earning less than $20,000, about $900 less for those in the $30,000 income bracket and about $1,300 less for the middle income family. There is no question that there are
many hidden penalties in the Government's changes to family benefits.
The House will recall that the primary change to child benefits was the partial deindexation of family allowances. The House will recall the debate on that issue. The children were unable to organize the way seniors organized in order to reindex pensions, so the Government proceeded to deindex family allowances while re-indexing pensions.
The increase in the child tax credit will be partially deindex-ed, by 1988, however, so that the threshold level will go down, fewer people will be eligible for the child tax credit and the amount will decrease.
The reduction of the child exemption, which has also been deindexed is particularly hard on the middle income family. These are subtle changes which particularly affect average income families.
As far as low income families are concerned, tax reform has not alleviated the increasing poverty of these families. There should have been a major increase in the child tax credit and it should have been fully indexed.
The sales tax hits poor families very hard because they must spend most of their welfare income on basic essentials like clothing, food and rent.
While child poverty has decreased dramatically, the tax measures even for poor families means $300 less in child benefits. We need an income security reform program, which is something that none of the Government programs have addressed. 1 have attempted to raise this question of poverty with the Minister of National Health and Welfare on a number of occasions.
It is misleading to suggest that poverty has gone down. While poverty among elderly people has decreased because old age pensions have risen-a Liberal initiative incidentally- child poverty has increased. It is a deplorable fact that one in five children in Canada goes to school hungry. We cannot even obtain a food program in Vancouver in order to assist poor children. It is deplorable that this country should depend on institutionalized food banks as a way of looking after our children. This Budget does little to help the situation at all.
Let me discuss the impact of this Budget on women. A press release issued by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women summarizes this very well. It states that the Budget does not deal with child care needs. They are very concerned that the federal Government is placing emphasis on deductions rather than on credits. Of course, deductions favour those who pay taxes and completely exclude those who do not pay taxes. This means that poor families do not have access to this tax measure.
They go on to state that deductions give greater benefits to higher income earners, and are an inappropriate use of tax dollars for child care. We agree with that.



February 22, 1988

They raise a very interesting point which I do not believe has been brought up in the House, that the proposals contained in the Budget related to alimony and maintenance payments run counter to the Council's recommendations in this area. They state:
We see no reason why a non-custodial parent can deduct amounts spent in support of children, while a custodial parent has no such right.
Why should fathers-mothers in a few cases-who are usually the higher income earners receive all the tax benefits while the mother who is struggling and is lucky if she receives those maintenance payment, does not have any tax benefits. The CACSW recommends that child support payments should be deductible by the lower-income earner, the spouse who is assuming care of the children directly.
The CACSW also talks about the $300 million a year for non-statutory spending. It feels that this could hit women's programs particularly including programs that prevent wife battering. Job creation and labour adjustment programs for women maybe jeopardized as well. It talks about the fact that
850,000	low-income people will be taken off the tax rolls by tax reform proposals but the Government does not mention, nor did the Minister who spoke recently, that at least one million low-income Canadians have joined the ranks of taxpayers over the past six years as a result of the limitation on indexing of the tax system. Again, the poor people are paying taxes and the wealthy people and corporations are paying very little or none.
The CACSW is concerned about indirect taxes and particularly about future changes proposed to the sales tax which again will have a regressive impact on women. The heaviest burden will be put on those least able to pay.
Finally, 1 would like to concentrate my remarks on the question of child care. We all know how important this program is. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that this would be a major social reform of his Government and he said close to three years ago now that there would be a major investment of money into quality child care spaces for families who need child care and who need it at rates they can afford to pay. However, that is the part that seems to have been forgotten by the Government's child care proposal.
We hear about regressive tax measures. The tax measures in this Budget will double the child care tax deduction for those who pay taxes from $2,000 to $4,000. That is nice for people with those kinds of expenses. This helps higher-income people who pay taxes, families with two professional parents. However, what about single mothers and low-income parents who desperately need to get into the workforce and have no benefits at all? They have been left out of that scheme. There is not even a tax credit for them.
Another program that is costly to Government revenues is the token, almost insulting payment of $100 this year to a parent who stays at home. No one can tell me that the value of
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
a homemaker who raises his or her own children is recognized by that. It would have been much sounder to have increased the child tax credit considerably for lower-income families.
As I mentioned to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), we are concerned that the Government is losing some $210 million this year in tax revenues as a result of these regressive tax measures but there is nothing in the Budget that will fulfil the promise, and it is only a promise, to put money directly into child care services. That is the first priority. Even families with increased tax deductions will have no guarantee that they will be able to find licensed, quality day care spaces for their children. Even if they do find the day care spaces, the fees will be high and the wages paid to care givers will be atrocious. Child car workers in Canada are paid approximately $15,000 per year in many instances, and that is an absolutely deplorable salary for trained professionals who are doing one of the most important jobs anyone could do by helping to raise a generation of children.
We are very disappointed that the Buget reinforced the regressive measures again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. I take note of the fact that Budget statistics indicate that corporate profits grew faster than other economic indicator. Corporate profits rose by 25.6 per cent over the last year. At the same time, corporate taxes rose by only 15.3 per cent.
I would like to know if taxes for average Canadians rose by less than their income rose. Are they being treated the same as corporations are being treated? Are there any Canadian families whose incomes rise more than their taxes?
The Budget indicates that 60,000 profitable corporations will continue to pay no corporate income tax. I wonder if my colleague is aware that in 1986, Alcan Aluminum made profits totalling $220 million but did not pay any taxes. Instead, it received a tax credit of $32 million. Does my colleague know that in 1986, Brascan, on profits totalling $187 million, received a tax credit of $2.3 million? The list goes on and on. I hesitate to read into the record all 60,000 examples.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. St. Julien
Does my colleague know of any families in her riding whose incomes have risen by more than their taxes have risen under the Conservative Government? Are families being treated the same as corporations?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. colleague has put onto the record some extremely significant figures. I hope he will expand on them when he makes his speech later in the day.
1 can think of only one kind of family in my riding whose incomes went up higher than their taxes did. Families on welfare might have gotten a few dollars per year more and pay no taxes at all. However, those families have used up all their income by the second week of the month and then have to line up at food banks because they have nothing to eat. Their children go to school hungry. I am sure there are not very many children of the management of Alcan and Brascan who find themselves in those situations.
If we had the income from fair taxes paid by 60,000 corporations, we could increase welfare rates and ensure that there are more child care spaces. We could ensure that children in Canada are not going to school hungry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be talking about the Budget, today. When we were elected, three and a half years ago, our greatest challenge was restoring financial stability and returning some credibility to the management of public finances. In 1984, the federal deficit and the national debt were out of control. The deficit was in excess of $38 billion, whereas three years previously it was only $14.9 billion. Over the same period, the national debt had doubled and was increasing at an average rate of 26 per cent per year. If we had continued at the same pace, it would be, today, $100 billion more than it is, which means $16,000 more for every family of four in the country.
Once the Government has lost control of its finances, everybody suffers. The interest rate applicable to mortgages, and consumer or business loans goes up. Confidence in the economy goes down, growth slows down and job creation decreases.
Mr. Speaker, our capability of providing the programs and services that Canadians need and want was in jeopardy. We believe Canadians want to leave their children and grandchildren a positive heritage, rich in opportunities, rather than a crushing debt and shattered expectations.
The only way to deal with that situation was to propose a short-term fiscal plan, providing for a sustained reduction of the deficit, and stick to it. That is exactly what we have done. We took a series of initiatives to put our finances in order by reducing federal spending and increasing revenues. Our first priority was to regain control of public spending.
In the four years before we came to office, program spending had increased at an average annual rate of 14 per cent, far in excess of the rate of inflation and enough to double spending in about five years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who wrote that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Since 1984, we managed to cut the average annual rate of increase in program spending to just 3.5 per cent, less than the inflation rate. We achieved this record because we have put in place a new, disciplined approach to the management of government and its finances.
We promised that we would each year cut the deficit. We have done so. We indicated that the control of expenditures would be the main source of deficit reduction. Such have been the case. For the current fiscal year, we predicted that the deficit would be cut to $29.3 billion and, according to the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson), that target will be met.
Mr. Speaker, we had promised to respond to the needs and priorities of Canadians in a fiscally responsible way. That is exactly what we did. When we took office in 1984, the country was in need of a sound financial management. This still is today and will remain in the future a foremost necessity. We must and will hold to our fiscal principles.
Firstly, we will reduce the growth rate of the national debt to that of the economy by 1990-91. Secondly, the annual deficit keeps declining steadily. In view of the forecasted decrease for 1988-89, it will be the first time ever since World War II that the deficit has declined four years in a row. Third, we are reducing Governement's financial needs to a considerable extent. Fourth, we are achieving most of that reduction through reduced spending and disciplined management.
With constant abiding by our fiscal principles and with structural improvements fostering economic growth, we managed to remain on the same financial course we have marked out since 1984.
Mr. Speaker, I would not miss that opportunity today to allude to a unique fact in Canadian history. That is the billions of dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money the Liberals have wasted. In September 1987, the Auditor General of Canada, Mr. Ken Dye, stated that because it took too much into consideration the political situation in Canada, the former Liberal Government had wasted, without any legitimate reason, billions of dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money.
The Ministry of Finance was made aware, in early 1984, that something was going wrong with the fiscal deduction program for scientific research. That warning was issued several times in the middle of that year. But that Department did not move because the Government was to go on an electoral campaign.
Had the Department of Finance stepped in earlier, according to Mr. Dye, it could have saved considerable amounts of money, something in the order of billions of dollars.
February 22, 1988

That controversial fiscal deduction program thus became the most costly fiscal disaster in the Canadian history. When announcing that program, in 1983, the former Minister of Finance, Mr. Marc Lalonde, predicted that it would cost only $200 million to the Government.
However, the program that was cancelled by the Tory Government shortly after the elections reached $3,9 billion. Up to $1,9 billion of that amount may have been lost as the result of frauds. There were some frauds where businesses and individuals claimed deductions without proceeding with any research. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the program was to provide generous tax deductions to encourage companies and individuals to invest in research and development. According to Mr. Dye, the Department of Finance should have had some misgivings from the beginning when there was an avalanche of registration forms as soon as the program was enforced in January, 1984. However, Mr. Lalonde was confident that the program would be effective. In L'actualite of February, 1987, journalist Paul Morisset wrote: "It is the theft of the century." In October 1984, the Tory successor to Marc Lalonde, the Minister of Finance, Michael Wilson, put a sudden stop to the whole matter. It was his first official act. However, it was already too late. In nine months, the bill had almost reached $3 billion, a tenth of the national deficit, enough to build more than 50 hospitals in Canada. According to the Minister of National Revenue, almost a dollar out of three was wasted, a billion disappeared through frauds and bankruptcies without being used for research.
Mr. Speaker, it was the worse fiscal fiasco in the history of Canada. How could such a disaster happen again? This question should be raised again at a time when Canadian taxpayers are filing their income tax returns and the government is launching its tax reform. I will give you a few examples, Mr. Speaker.
In Calgary, a businessman received $30 million; he bought two office buildings, a Jaguar and a 160-acre ranch before he vanished.
Another example, Mr. Speaker: in Kitchener, Ontario, half a dozen foreign businessmen got $2.5 million to build high-technology mini-submarines. They left with the money but without a forwarding address. The plans submitted to officials were drawings of submarines from the Second World War!
One last example, Mr. Speaker: in Montreal, the Department was investigating three companies implicated in dubious transactions totalling between $15 and $20 million and involving the same individuals. In this popular scheme, the whole building is claimed as an R and D expense while only one room out of 10 floors is used as a laboratory. Or a contractor erects a $4 million building, gets $8 million from the owner and submits a $30 million invoice for tax purposes.
Then there were some tax evaders who paid university professors from $5,000 to $10,000 to write serious-looking proposals. The bigger the projects, the more dubious they tended to be. But there were two big problems: first of all, the
The Budget-Mr. St. Julien
government was signing blank cheques. It was giving out tax credits without really checking and before research started. The claimant only had to fill out a short form. The Department of Finance officials wanted a flexible system free from red tape.
The other problem, Mr. Speaker, were the quick flips allowed under the program. In short, the investor paid the money and got half back the next day to make a 5 to 10 per cent profit in 24 hours without any risk! Three quarters of the money invested in the SRIC Program was used for quick flips.
In an interview, Marc Lalonde stated: "Obviously, there were some abuses ..." It is clear that the law was not tight enough. But out of $3 billion, $2 million went to research. I say: "Hear, hear!"
Mr. Speaker, it is not one but 1.9 billion that have been lost because of cheating. Who is responsible for all that mess? The Minister is always responsible for his programs, said Marc Lalonde himself. I never believed in blaming my officials.
From early June 1984, less than five months after the official announcement of the tax credit, he had more than enough evidence that the program was going off the deep end. He had the power to stop everything and to save hundreds of millions of dollars to the tax payers. He preferred to swagger.
Mr. Speaker, why is it that the then Prime Minister of Canada and present leader of the Liberal Opposition did not put an end to these tax frauds? Why is it that the Opposition parties do not ask today that a Royal Commission be created to examine these frauds? I will conclude here on these tax frauds, Mr. Speaker, since 1 could speak on that all day long.
To continue, Mr. Speaker, there is another budget related issue which is of great interest to me and to Northern residents. Last February 11, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) said in this House: "1 have had the opportunity to visit-the area of Abitibi, of Val-d'Or, and I am always amazed at seeing that Members of Parliament for that region do not protest more vehemently against the decisions taken by the Minister concerning the elimination of flow-through shares." Unfortunately, the Hon. Member is misinformed about what 1 do. In any case, when he went to Rouyn-Noranda for the annual meeting of Quebec prospectors in 1987, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides arrived at night fall and left that very same evening. Where was he last December 20, when a meeting was organized to save flowthrough shares? I was the only federal Member of Parliament there.
Mr. Speaker, at the end of 1986, the Quebec Government lowered the maximum deduction from 166 and 2/3 to 133 and 1/3 per cent. This initiative, coupled with the minimum tax introduced in 1985, made mining inflation hedges less attractive, but the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides and his Quebec Liberal colleagues have remained very silent about this cut back in Quebec.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. St. Julien
In any case, 1 am still working to maintain flow-through shares and I have made public statements on that issue both in Ottawa and in my own constituency.
The major difference between the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides and myself is that he was in Abitibi only for a few hours, as a tourist.
In the Budget speech of February 10, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said the following about regional development:
We are also implementing a new approach to regional development-
-in Canada and Quebec-
-an approach that will be more responsive to needs and priorities in the
regions. It will draw fully on the ideas and the initiative of people living in the
various regions as we work to achieve more balanced development across
Canada.
There is now a plan for the Atlantic region, one for Western Canada and one for Northern Ontario. The Government has also announced its intention to respond more effectively to the real development needs of remote and less prosperous regions in Quebec, For this purpose, an in depth consultation process will be undertaken with the people of the regions, representatives of local business and of the provincial Government.
I am very happy at the announcement made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) at a press conference in Sept-Iles on December 22 about the five-year economic development plan which the Mulroney Government will be implementing to stimulate regional initiative and eliminate once and for all regional disparities.
Indeed, until the mid 80s, Quebec peripheral regions had been neglected by the Canadian Government. The federal regional development efforts in Quebec were strongly concentrated on the more industrialized regions in the southwest region of the province. Eastern Quebec was the only outlying region whose development was managed under a distinct, multisectorial and multi-year program, based on the analysis of the strenghts and the weaknesses of the regional economy and on the determination of the most promising development lines.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, North West Quebec, the Saguenay- Lac-Saint-Jean and the North Shore, as much as the Gaspe- Lower-Saint-Lawrence and Magdalen Islands, had then and still have particular needs. Economic development there is more costly and more difficult to manage than elsewhere. These isolated regions, far from the marketplace with their scattered and very mobile population, their total reliance on natural resources whose development is subject to the fluctuations of international demand and foreign competition, allow us to look into the development problems common to those vast economic areas which represent close to 90 per cent of Quebec territory.
Therefore, as of the Fall of 1984, the new government team headed by the Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Mulroney) put the outlying regions of Quebec among its regional
development priorities. The sub-agreements concluded in 1985 under the Canada-Quebec Economic and Regional Development Agreement, although essentially sector-oriented, have led to major financial commitments in the outlying regions, particularly to enhance mining and forest development and to strenghten transportation infrastructure. Major national policies, such as the free-trade agreement with the United States, have created more favourable conditions for the development of Quebec resource areas. Ad hoc actions, such as the establishment of a federal penitentiary in Port-Cartier and financial support for the paper mill in Matane, were also intended to promote employment growth in those regions.
For this new plan to be realistic, Mr. Speaker, namely to overcome the regional development problems experienced in those areas, it should aim at accelerating long-term growth by mobilizing local entrepreneurs, by stimulating the development and the processing of our natural resources, by promoting excellence and technological development, by encouraging diversification of our regional economic stucture, by promoting the full integration of regions to Canadian and North American economies.
The new global plan will aim at four fronts: Eastern Quebec, the North Shore, Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean and Northwest Quebec. Each will have its own funding to ensure that development initiatives meet the needs of each area.
The plan would last a minimum of five years because a regional development effort cannot have any structuring and durable effect unless it is sustained and coherent. Previous experience clearly reflected that peacemeal and short-term solutions give poor results.
For each of the targeted areas, the development plan would be articulated around five major fields of operation in the master plan consistent with the major concerns of the Federal Government and of the area with regard to regional development, namely technological research and development, business development, the development of natural resources, of human resources and infrastructures.
too)
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that when I arrived in Abitibi in 1984, the unemployment rate was about 22, 23 and 25 percent in my constituency as in most of the towns and villages. We now have the lowest unemployment rate ever, 6.6 per cent, unheard of! We owe that to both federal and provincial programs, to the two levels of Government, to the private sector, to our employers, and to all workers in our region.
We have to keep this economic renewal going, for we all recall that the rate had invariably hovered around 20 and 25 per cent in previous years. We did find a formula, we now have flow-through shares, a very complex matter as we all know, but I do not hold back in my statements in Ottawa or in my riding. Between now and June our Government will have to
February 22, 1988

take a much closer look and make a change, come up with a new formula to help our Quebec prospectors.
We also have a sector where two military bases are to be closed down, including one at Senneterre where people are experiencing troubled times. The federal Government and the Government of Quebec must synchronize their efforts to give additional assistance to Senneterre.
We know that our Government launched a community development program under which they were allocated $200,000 over the first two years to set up an office. And again recently, last week in fact, we earmarked $1.3 million to include both projects in the community development program.
In my riding we have three other projects, specifically in Amos, Matagami and Chapais-Chibougamau.
Mr. Speaker, 1 suggest we will have to work very hard to sustain such economic growth and keep unemployment down to 6.6 per cent. That is precisely what our Government will do to keep the economic renewal going.
