subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. Questions and comments?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his speech the Hon. Member stressed the problems we had with the former scientific research tax credit.
He knows perfectly well that this tax credit was introduced to help high tech companies that always have trouble obtaining risk capital.
The companies themselves asked for this kind of program to help them obtain the initial financing they require to develop new products.
As 1 said before, the Hon. Member stressed the problems that arose as a result of this program, and he failed to mention, or mentioned only briefly, that the program did help develop a lot of good research that will benefit Canadians and the Canadian economy, and will increase innovation in the private sector.
He may also be aware that companies are now asking for a similar program to be introduced, but with adequate controls. I don't know whether he attended the National Conference on Science, Technology and Innovation, where the private sector was very emphatic about the need for setting up such a program with the control mechanisms that were lacking in the former program.
However, I would like to ask a question about the Government's present program which was introduced by the Conservative Government, and I am referring to the refundable tax credit in the 1985 Budget. In fact, the tax credit as such already existed, but this Government increased the refund available under the program. The Hon. Member must know that the program is having quite a few problems because of very tight restrictions imposed by Revenue Canada. 1 may refer him to an article that appeared in Le Soleil on February
The Budget-Mr. St. Julien
16, under the heading: Revenue Canada discourages research. This was in response to a CP press release which referred to Revenue Canada's rigorous approach that was discouraging R and D in advanced technology.
The article followed a survey of 212 companies conducted by the Canadian Advanced Technology Association. The survey revealed that many companies had to wait for as long as twelve or eighteen months before receiving their tax credit refund. I am aware of some very serious situations where companies have had to close down because of the long delay involved in getting their refunds, and it is not just the delay but the incertainty about whether or not they actually will obtain a refund. In many cases, Revenue Canada will not accept the research expenditures incurred by many of these companies as such. There is some confusion about the definition of "research".
Is the Hon. Member aware of these problems? Could he inform the House what he intends to do to ensure the program meets the needs of Canada's private sector?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the Hon. Member for Laurier. The House is aware that he represents the smallest riding in Canada with an area of five square kilometers, and that I represent the largest of the ten provinces in Canada with an area of 740,000 square kilometers. In other words, there are 60,000 people in his riding, while there are 102,000 in mine.
But to return to the Hon. Member's question about the difficulties companies are experiencing when trying to get reimbursements for their research activities, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that after the 1983-84 scandal of the century, and I refer here to the article which Paul Morisset wrote in L'Actualite in 1987 about the shortfall of $1 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

He mentioned the part played by lawyers and accountants:
There were other expenditures. The Department of National Revenue has indicated that some $350 million in honoraria were paid to lawyers, accountants and brokers of all sorts.
-that is to say-

The newspaper continues in the same vein:
Auditor General Kenneth Dye, the taxpayers' watchdog in Ottawa

at the time-
-compared the Members of the House with a team of engineers trying to develop a car which is not a gas guzzler: "They think they have succeeded, but the engine seems to swallow up as much gas as before.

They just cannot understand, until they discover a large number of very

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To my Hon. friend who is urging us to investigate the scandals, I need only remind him of the greatest robbery of the century. We will hold a royal inquiry on this. But the Hon. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The time for questions and comments is now over. Debate. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that 1 welcome the opportunity to participate in the budget debate. The Budget which the Government has brought down really says a lot to Canadians. It tells us a lot about the Government's priorities and policies.
To any ordinary citizen the budgetary papers may look like quite a pile of paper. Of course half of it is in English and half is in French. Previous Budgets consisted of larger stacks of paper. It was very difficult for opposition Members to go through them in a matter of a few hours. Therefore, we have the lock-up which allows some of our representatives to be briefed for many hours.
This Budget is a flimsy one. This Budget does very little. This Budget shows that the Government is bankrupt of ideas. This is a "do-nothing Budget". This Budget is an excuse for a budget. This Budget is not really a budget.
Budget day just came along and the Government said, "Oh, we have to produce a budget. The Minister of Finance has to buy a new pair of shoes. He has to get his picture in the papers showing the good soles on his shoes and he has to say something". The Government managed to put together a speech which did not say anything. It talked about all the good things the Government has done. It painted a rosy picture of the economy. However, in the final analysis, this is no budget
whatsoever. It certainly does not respond to the concerns and needs of ordinary Canadians.
I have spent some considerable time meeting and talking with people in their homes. I must say that they delivered a message to me which I feel a responsibility to deliver to the House and to the Government. Canadians want to know if anybody is listening to them. They want to know if anybody will speak up for them. They would be curious to know if anybody on the government front-bench is speaking for them. In a nutshell Canadians have said, "Enough is enough. We are taking home less pay. You are increasing our taxes. You are a burden on our backs. Get off our backs; enough is enough".
1 want to touch on a few aspects of the Budget and to talk about taxes on corporations. I want to talk about Canadian families and I want to say a few more things about what the Budget tells us about Conservative policy and about the Mulroney Government's approach to Government.
First, with regard to corporations, I noted earlier today, and I want to note once again, that statistics from the Budget indicate that profits for Canadian corporations have gone up by some 25.6 per cent. I do not know any families in my riding whose income has gone up by 25.6 per cent. Most people in my riding and most Canadians across the country have a hard time getting an increase of 3 per cent. They get 4 per cent if they are lucky. Corporation profits have gone up by 25.6 per cent which is the biggest rise of any economic indicator.
Although I am a New Democrat, I do not begrudge corporations their profits. I must say though that when they do make profits they ought to be good corporate citizens and pay a fair share of the taxation burden which Canadian families have to pay. Why is it that when corporations profits go up by
25.6	per cent their taxes only increased by 15.3 per cent? What happened to the other 10 per cent? Which ordinary Canadian family can say to us "My income has increased by 25 per cent over the past year but my taxes have not kept pace?" The people in my riding are telling me that their taxes are going up faster than their incomes. They are fed up and they are saying "Get off my back, Brian Mulroney. We are sick and tired of farcical tax reform which promised lower taxes but is resulting in increased taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will come back to the point I made earlier. Corporate profits in this country have gone up by
25.6	per cent while their taxes have gone up by only 15.3 per cent. At the same time under Tory rule 60,000-not 60, not 600, but 60,000 corporations in Canada continue to pay no taxes on their profits. We are not saying that we should starve corporations, but we are saying that when corporations make profits as members of the community they ought to pay taxes.
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
I want to point out to Hon. Members who jump up to their feet on points of order that they ought to deal with this question. Do they know that in 1986 Alcan Aluminum on profits of $220 million, rather than paying taxes received a tax credit of $32 million? What ordinary Canadian family can get a deal like that? In the same year, Brascan, another Canadian corporation, on profits totalling $187 million paid no taxes but received a tax credit of $2.3 million. Brascan was given money. In 1986 Hees International, on profits totalling $117 million paid-guess what-no taxes. Power Financial earned profits of $132 million and received a tax credit of $1 million. The list goes on. While the profits of corporations mount, their taxes do not keep pace but ordinary Canadian families are being asked to pay more and more.
What Canadians want to know is just who is this Conservative Government listening to? Who does it care for? What does its policies tell us about who the Government is interested in and who it is serving? What are the priorities of the Government? The Government's actions speak louder than its words. Its actions indicate that it bows and scrapes when it comes to large and powerful corporations, large and powerful private interests, but when it comes to ordinary families, the Government lays on the tax burden. The Government does not hear the calls for help and relief from ordinary Canadians.
I do not know whether Members in this House know, or whether Members of the Government side know, but certainly the people in my riding know that the Budget which the Government brought down and the previous budgets it has brought down since its election have hit the middle-class family the hardest. Middle class Canadians have reached the end of their rope. We hear them saying "We have no more disposable income. Four or five years ago we used to have a few dollars in our pockets. We had some change and some discretionary income. That has now gone." The Conservative Government continues to raise taxes, continues to increase the burden, and still has not heard the pleas of ordinary Canadians for relief.
I want to quote a little documentation in this regard just in case someone may doubt what I have to say. I hope that the jolly Members on the other side will get up and join this debate and explain these taxation policies. The Canadian Council on Social Development says:
One segment of the Canadian population which has not advanced during this government's term is families with dependent children.
What is a family without children? Those are the people who have not advanced under the present Government. The Canadian Council on Social Development goes on to say:
Starting with the 1985 Budget and continuing through to the tax reform proposals, families with children have lost ground compared with other Canadian households. The effects of partially deindexing all family benefit programs and tax credits, in conjunction with tax reform measures, will mean that a one-earner couple with two kids and an income of $30,000 will pay $1,439 more in total income and federal consumption taxes in 1990 than in

February 22, 1988
1984, after adjusting for inflation. By comparison, a similar couple with no
kids will pay $975 more.
That certainly does not jibe with the music we hear from the Government which talks about income tax reductions. The reality is not the Government's rhetoric but rather that taxes are continuing to increase, particularly on the backs of Canadian families.
Why is that when Canadians' incomes are being held down, when they have a difficult time getting a 1, 2, 3, or 4 per cent increase, their burden of taxes continues to increase while at the same time corporate profits soar and their taxes lag behind the rate at which their incomes increase? Who is the Conservative Government interested in? Who is it listening to? Is there anyone on the front bench of the Conservative Government who is willing to speak up for ordinary families or are they all going to repeat the party line?
There is one other aspect of the experience of ordinary Canadians which 1 want to bring to the attention of the House and the Government. I will quote again from the documentation of the Canadian Council on Social Development to show a reality which this House must acknowledge and which ordinary Canadians know from their own personal experience by looking at their pay cheques. The document reads:
Trends in average wages and salaries between 1983 and 1987 also reflect the
lower pay attached to Canadian jobs. In real terms, workers today take home
on average $8.60 a week less than in 1983.
The income of the average Canadian family is dropping at the same time as the Government continues to increase the burden on Canadian families. It is the middle class family, the average Canadian family, which is being hit the hardest. Everyone is losing, whether they are poor, working class, or middle class, but the average Canadian family is being hit the hardest. It is time for this to stop. It is time for the Government to stop coddling the corporations while slamming the families of the country. It is time for some fairness in the taxation system rather than the sham of tax reform which the Government presents to the Canadian people.
I have one message for the Government which comes directly from my constituents, and that is, enough is enough, get off our backs. The Government is supposed to serve people and not to hurt them. Leave the average Canadian family alone.

subsubtopic: NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES-ELIGIBILITY OF ONTARIO COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in December last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a special tax reduction package for residents of northern and isolated areas. Several communities in the constituency of Cochrane-Superior are unable to claim these deductions on their 1987 income tax returns. I submit that the reason for their exclusion is extremely narrow in concept.
As the regulations now stand, they do not reflect the realities of northern Ontario. For example, there are communities which score high on points for geography, population, access, and they lack many services but because they are just a few kilometres short of the required 320 kilometres from a major centre they are out of luck. Surely a community which otherwise is over qualified for the tax reduction should not be left out in the cold because of a few kilometres.
Accordingly, I have asked the Minister of Finance to make distance a part of the point system. In this way, on the one hand the communities in question would be included, and on the other hand the system would not be open for abuse. 1 therefore urge the Minister of Finance to introduce the appropriate changes to the regulations without delay.

Mr. Speaker, Olympics 88 have brought plaudits from all over the world to Calgary, Alberta and Canada. The opening show and each event that followed were sparkling, scintillating, glittering, wonderful, miraculous, marvelous, prodigious, spectacular, fabulous,
February 22, 1988

thrilling, fascinating, beautiful, exquisite, enchanting and inspiring. A small boy clapping his hands and with shining eyes put it best when he shouted: "Boy! That was real cool!".
The hundreds of volunteers, the committees, the performers, the athletes and all others who contributed should share the glory and the credit. The athletes, men and women from all over the world, of all colours, religions and creeds, each competing for the Gold, thrilled us as winners and losers congratulated each other in real sportsmanlike style.
To the Hon. Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek), Mayor Ralph Klein, Frank King and all others who carried the responsibilities of this world event, Canadians say: "Thank you for the best Winter Olympics the world has ever seen".

subtopic: NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES-COMMISSION OF INQUIRY URGED
NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES-COMMISSION OF INQUIRY URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government recently released its comprehensive list of prescribed communities which qualify for northern residents tax deduction.
The result for many ridings is a complicated patchwork of have and have-not residents whose tax returns bear no relation to the principle of fairness and to the need for a northern tax allowance.
Northerners pay more for virtually everything, from gasoline and home heating fuel to transportation and cable television services. In almost every case, they therefore pay more in fixed taxes.
At the same time northerners do not have access to many of the public services accorded to residents in the south. Whether we speak of colleges or universities, subways and baseball stadiums, northerners do not receive the same benefits for their tax dollar. Northerners do not deserve to be sliced and diced into a checkerboard of so-called remote and non-remote communities. 1 call for the creation of a commission of inquiry to examine this matter, and I look forward to representing all my constituents before the committee.
However, the tax season is upon us. The only fair way to help northern taxpayers this year is to designate all communities in Tier 3 ridings as isolated and remote.

Mr. Speaker, this week marks the 60th anniversary of the Cercle national des journalistes du Canada a la Chambre des communes et au Parlement du Canada. In honour of this event, tomorrow the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) will inaugurate the Cercle's mini-museum and an exhibition: "Aperfu: Phoenix sur la Colline" at the Public Archives of Canada, a photographic account of the Parliament Centre Block fire in February 1916.
Wednesday, plaques honouring the founders of the Cercle, The Citizen and Le Droit will be unveiled during a special ceremony. Former employees and representatives of the founding newspapers and former presidents of le Cercle will be among the guests.
The week's festivities will conclude on Friday and Saturday with a musical review of press and politicians over the years.
Mr. Speaker, sixty years of journalism in Ottawa, including radio and television as well as the written press, is something to celebrate. Congratulations to one and all!

Mr. Speaker, last week we heard that the last postal strike cost Canada Post $70 million. While the Corporation is trying to close down rural post offices and depriving thousands of Canadians of home delivery, Canada Post, thanks to its arrogant policies, spent a total of $70 million during the last postal strike alone, and it seems that a few months before, the first mail carriers' strike cost another $30 million. Mr. Speaker, $100 million was wasted on strikes that failed to solve any problems at all. On the contrary, the situation keeps getting worse, and labour relations at Canada Post have become extremely tense.
1 think the Government should recognize its responsibility and instruct Canada Post to treat its employees like human beings, to sit down at the same table and act responsibly. Mail delivery is everybody's business, Mr. Speaker, not just that of Canada Post. The Corporation should publish its figures so that everybody can see for themselves what is going on.

February 22, 1988

subtopic: REFUGEE STATUS GRANTED TO TERRORIST IN 1977
REFUGEE STATUS GRANTED TO TERRORIST IN 1977
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently Canadians have learned that another extremely dangerous terrorist was admitted to Canada in 1977. The individual from Argentina is presently serving a prison term for drug trafficking.
What is of major concern is that this individual was granted refugee status by the Refugee Appeal Board, when this body had in its possession the evidence which made this individual inadmissible to Canada.
This is not the first time that this Board has made decisions which may be detrimental to Canada. One wonders how many other individuals who could severely jeopardize the lives of innocent Canadians have been admitted to Canada.
The Minister should undertake a review of all cases which were considered to be high risk, but were given approval by the Refugee Board. Remember that the terrorists know no boundaries, and that Canadians have already experienced terrorist acts. The Air-lndia tragedy is a reasonable example.
With the Olympics now in progress and the economic conference slated for June, a review is urgent. The safety of Canadians must always be the primary concern of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, today Scarborough City Council is standing up to Canada Post. It is saying no to the so-called supermailboxes in spite of implied threats of poor service.
Canadians want to know when the Government will stand up to Canada Post. We know that the Tory Government and Canada Post have embarked on a policy of eliminating door-to-door service in new areas. When will they turn to existing areas and eliminate service there? Are they building a case for eliminating door-to-door service in all urban areas? What happened to the concept of fairness? Why does one neighbourhood receive service while another does not? Why are senior citizens and handicapped people required to use these boxes rather than have mail delivered to their doors?
It is time for the Government to stand up to Canada Post rather than leaving the job to Scarborough City Council.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to acquaint the House with a rather funny situation: Mr. Remy Trudel, who is Dean of Quebec University in Abitibi-Temis-camingue, has officially joined the NDP ranks in anticipation of the forthcoming election.
Moreover, while still exercising his duties, Dean Trudel spends his time travelling everywhere in Quebec as the big whig responsible for recruiting candidates for the socialist party. He should resign his position as Dean in Rouyn-Noranda. What is he waiting for? Is he not in a conflict of interest situation, Mr. Speaker? In his position as Dean how could he objectively analyze the university assistance programs implemented by the Government?
Mr. Speaker, is Dean Trudel using his generous expense accounts to travel everywhere in Quebec sowing the seed of socialism in our province? I suggest the Quebec Government should examine the current status-an embarrassing one, to say the least-of the Dean of Quebec University in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. If he wants to fight against the Government of Quebec and the Government of Canada, he should give up to someone not politically involved his comfortable and well-paid position at the expense of Quebec taxpayers.
The House is aware that the NDP is a political party which operates at both provincial and federal levels at the same time. The Socialists who are Members of the NDP are not in a position to give anybody a lecture on conflict of interests and honesty.

maintopic: STUDY SHOWING LEUKEMIA INCREASE IN PERSONS LIVING NEAR NUCLEAR INSTALLATIONS
STUDY SHOWING LEUKEMIA INCREASE IN PERSONS LIVING NEAR NUCLEAR INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a British study conducted last summer reveals a higher incidence of leukemia and an increased number of leukemia-related deaths among children and young adults living near nuclear installations.
The National Cancer Institute in the United States announced that a similar study will be conducted there in the next nine months, to find any hot spots, or areas with an unusually large number of cancers.
A spokesman for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Mr. Mac Keillor, is reported to have said that no Canadian
February 22, 1988

research is being undertaken, that the British study is outdated, and that it has been refuted by other studies. This statement is disturbing, considering the fact that the findings of the British study are significant enough for the U.S. National Cancer Institute to conduct a similar study. We therefore urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to wake up and launch such a study in Canada because we cannot afford any delay.

subtopic: BEEF CARCASSES-PRICES CHARGED BY PACKING HOUSES
BEEF CARCASSES-PRICES CHARGED BY PACKING HOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in September, 1987, the federal Department of Agriculture changed the grading of beef carcasses so that a half inch of back fat lowered the grade from A1 to A2. Department meat inspectors have done a good job and have graded according to the new rules. It appears that the packing houses are taking advantage of both producers and consumers by charging retailers the same price for A1 and A2 beef carcasses.
The difference in price varies from five cents to eight cents per pound, or about $30 to $50 per animal. Packers do not pay for the hide, liver and other saleable parts of the animal. Surely the producers should get the benefit refunded to them if the meat packers are not going to pass this lower cost onto the consumers.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have a long way to go yet before we know fully how to deal with the epidemic of AIDS. However, one thing is becoming clear. For a person who has AIDS or is knowingly a carrier of it, there should be a special duty to avoid communicating it to others.
In The Ottawa Citizen over the weekend, I read another story of a person with AIDS knowingly giving blood. I think it ought to be drawn to the attention of police departments across the country that criminal negligence is defined in the Criminal Code and well covers this type of situation in which wanton or reckless disregard for the lives and safety of other persons is shown. I would urge the police to use this section of the law to enforce a higher duty of responsibility on those who have AIDS or who are AIDS carriers than they presently seem disposed to use.

maintopic: S. 0. 21 RAILWAYS BRANCH LINE REHABILITATION PROGRAM-OMISSION OF WOOD MOUNTAIN SUBDIVISION
S. 0. 21 RAILWAYS BRANCH LINE REHABILITATION PROGRAM-OMISSION OF WOOD MOUNTAIN SUBDIVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday elements of the 1988-89 rail branch line rehabilitation program were announced. Unfortunately no mention was made of the Wood Mountain subdivision, a 65-mile CP line between Ogle and Mankota in southern Saskatchewan.
Elevators on this line have been handling some four million bushels of grain annually. The alternative involves trucking grain distances of 30 miles or more over difficult terrain.
Many past studies, including the Prairie Rail Action Committee's, have supported retention and upgrading of the Wood Mountain line, as have the grain companies and the railway. As part of the permanent rail network, users have been led to believe that upgrading to hopper car standards would continue, some $3.4 million already having been spent for this purpose.
Area residents cannot help but be concerned with what appears to be a change of plans concerning this line. They ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to review this entire matter and to consider reinstating the Wood Mountain subdivision in the 1988 rehab program.

Mr. Speaker, once again I am required to rise in the House to point out how the federal Government is neglecting its responsibilities to our native people. I have often risen in this place before to complain of the housing that our native people are offered by the federal Government. My constituents and I are fed up with these conditions and we demand that they cease.
Native people in northern Canada live in substandard housing because of rules set by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. These rules are entirely out of line with conditions in the North. They do not allow for the types of costs that occur in the North. The system does not offer the necessary flexibility to these isolated communities and there is simply not enough money available to correct the horrendous conditions that exist, or even to maintain what is already there.
Housing provided by the Department of Indian Affairs is deplorable, inadequate and a national disgrace. The backlog in needed houses ensures that the problem will not be solved in this century. Now is the time for action.
In Manitoba the provincial Government has been working hard to ensure that adequate housing is available to native

February 22, 1988
Oral Questions
people. Once again 1 call upon the federal Government to improve its commitment. It is time for the federal Government to act to correct this horrendous situation.

subtopic: BLACK HISTORY MONTH-RECORD OF SERVICE TO CANADA
BLACK HISTORY MONTH-RECORD OF SERVICE TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this month is Black History Month in North America. Many believe that blacks have been in Canada for only about 20 years. In fact the first blacks came to New France in 1628. Blacks were among the United Empire Loyalists who settled in Canada 200 years ago and they distinguished themselves in both the War of 1812 and the Upper Canada Rebellion. From 1820 to 1865, almost 50,000 fugitive slaves obtained their freedom in Canada by way of the famous underground railway.
The first black Canadian doctor was born in Toronto in 1837. A black Canadian woman published a newspaper in Chatham, Ontario, in 1850. A black Canadian served as a Toronto alderman for 13 consecutive years from 1894 to 1907, and a black Canadian lawyer was appointed a King's Counsel in 1910.
Today there are approximately 263,000 black Canadians. They did not just arrive. They have been Canadians for over 350 years and they continue to make an outstanding and growing contribution to our country.

subtopic: LANGUAGE TEACHERS-GUARANTEED TIME FOR PREPARATION OF COURSES
LANGUAGE TEACHERS-GUARANTEED TIME FOR PREPARATION OF COURSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
Treasury Board officials insist that language teachers should give every week up to 37.5 hours of instruction, thereby denying them any time to prepare their classes. Such a situation does not exist anywhere else in this country. In fact, this is a repressive measure against a professional group which is much too visibly involved with spreading bilingualism within the Public Service. This is a largely Francophone group the members of which are mostly women.
The Government claims that it wants to save money! There is nothing to say against that, for bilingualism, like the Treasury Board itself, will never be cost efficient. The greatest benefit we can expect from them is a greater measure of justice in Public Service job accessibility to reflect national unity.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I would like to know when and how the Government intends to introduce legislation implementing the Prime Minister's trade deal with the United States. Last week representatives of President Reagan and leaders of the Congress agreed that American legislation on the deal would be drafted jointly by the administration and the Congress. Then in a letter from the U.S. trade representative and the Secretary of the Treasury to the leaders of the Congress dated February 17, the President's cabinet members said the following:
Obviously, the President cannot make an absolute guarantee that he will be
bound to legislation that has not yet been drafted, just as you cannot guarantee
Congressional approval of such legislation.
It is therefore obvious that neither the administration nor the Congress knows yet what will be in the legislation. Can I have a commitment from the Prime Minister that he will not try to push legislation implementing that trade deal through the House at least until Canadians have had an opportunity to see what the administration and the United States Congress come up with?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that the Leader of the Opposition would have been eager for an opportunity to debate and oppose the legislation. Now he is apparently asking for some delay and that we not bring it forward. I suppose that would give an opportunity for someone to return from Washington to report back on the latest Liberal position in respect of this important trade matter.
I can tell my right hon. friend that the legislation appropriate to Canada is now being drafted and it will be tabled at an appropriate time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some of my colleagues indeed were in Washington last week getting more information from the Congress and the administration than we ever get from this Government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we also learned that the American Congress is currently considering two versions of a massive omnibus Trade Bill that will have a dramatic effect on Canada. Nowhere in either version of this prospective legislation is there so much as a word exempting Canada from the protectionist provisions of that Bill.
Does the Prime Minister have a guarantee from the President or from the leaders of the Congress that Canada will


February 22, 1988

be specifically exempted from the American omnibus trade legislation? If he does not, what is the point of proceeding with that deal and implementing it in the House of Commons when the country can be dramatically affected in a negative way by this omnibus trade legislation?

Mr. Speaker, the predictions of cataclysmic events by the Leader of the Opposition very rarely occur, either predictions of economic growth or job creation in Canada. 1 suspect he will be equally off the mark in regard to trade.
We have our obligation, having concluded a sovereign agreement, to bring forward appropriate legislation, and we shall. The Americans have a similar agreement. It is my understanding that they shall do likewise,, and at an appropriate time my right hon. friend will be able to deal with the facts as opposed to speculation coming from one of his travelling salesmen in Washington.

It is because we want to deal with facts that we would like to know what is in that legislation as it is negotiated by the Congress of the United States and the President. We will want to know whether Canada will be exempted from the omnibus trade legislation. Without that the trade deal will not be worth the paper it is printed on. The Prime Minister knows that.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last November the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion committed the federal Government to establish a duty remission program for the textile industry.
Given the resolution adopted by the Conference of American Governors, now we know that the governors along with American officials and a number of American congressmen do not want the Canadian Government to help the Canadian textile industry because that will have an impact on the American industry.
Is the reason why we do not have a program to help our textile industry the fact that the Prime Minister is afraid to provoke a negative reaction on the part of the Americans?

Mr. Speaker, I should advise the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that the Government has a number of programs in place to help the clothing and textile industry. We have been in discussions with members of the industry which pre-date the signing of the trade agreement back in October. These discussions are continuing in ways that will help the industry retain and improve upon its competitive position. When there is need for further announcements those announcements will be made.

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PROTECTION OF JOBS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. There are 86,000 workers in the textile sector, and 80 per cent of them are women. In keeping with an article in the Canada-U.S. agreement, the Government promised job protection to textile workers. Would the Prime Minister assure the House of Commons today that the Government intends to honour this specific commitment?

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PROTECTION OF JOBS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think that that is really the same question. The Hon. Member is coming at it from a somewhat different direction than that of the Leader of the Opposition and his colleague, the House Leader. We have indicated quite clearly that we are continuing the discussions with the industry in helping it maintain and improve its competitive position and improve the ability of the industry to create jobs in Canada. Those discussions are continuing, and they involve a number of Ministers of the Government.
As I said in response to a previous question, when an announcement is ready to be made it will be made.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to pursue what the Minister has said and what he said earlier in answer to the Leader of the Opposition. He said earlier in Question Period that the Government had been negotiating a special arrangement before this deal was entered into. The Minister will know that since October the Government made a very specific proposal, one that the Canadian industry is well aware of, and about which the Minister who is directly responsible said in the House about two weeks ago is consistent with the terms of the agreement.
Since then, incredible as it may seem, it has been reported that the Canadian Ambassador in Washington has now joined with American Governors and a number of American Senators
in urging Canada to scrap this protective measure for our workers in the textile industry.
I want to ask the Minister, who apparently is answering either for the Prime Minister or for the Minister for International Trade today, to confirm the report that the Canadian Ambassador has made this request. Will he assure the House that that request will be denied and that the Canadian Government will adhere to its original commitment to the textile workers?

Mr. Speaker, we have indicated quite clearly by including in the terms of the free trade agreement a provision which allows for duty remission schemes. That commitment is there, which is what I have indicated. A number of Ministers and myself are discussing it with the industry. It is a matter that is under discussion in order to try to improve and to assist the industry to maintain its competitive position and to create the jobs that both the Hon. Member and I are very much in favour of creating. Those discussions are continuing. As I have indicated, when there is a resolution of those discussions announcements will be made.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is frequently quite forthright in his answers, whether one agrees with him or not. He does answer the questions. But he ignored two specific questions that I put to him.
First, will he confirm that the Canadian Ambassador in Washington has requested that the Government scrap its proposal, which proposal has been discussed or outlined in detail to the Canadian industry? Will he tell the House whether or not the Canadian Ambassador has done that?
Second, will he assure us that the specific proposal with respect to the duty remission scheme which has been discussed since October will be kept in place so that Canadian jobs in this industry will at least be protected in a way that is consistent with the accord that the Government has negotiated with the United States?

Mr. Speaker, let me make it quite clear that what we will be doing will be consistent with both the spirit and the terms of the free trade agreement. The Hon. Member is attaching a good deal of precision to the discussions that have been going on. I should say to him that we have not reached a stage where there is that degree of precision. There are a range of things that are being discussed.
As I have indicated, when we have reached some resolution of these discussions, then there will be an announcement.
February 22, 1988

I then referred to other companies, including Brascan, Hees International, Power Financial, Xerox Canada, Total Petroleum, Wardair and PWA. The list goes on.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
1 assume from the question that my hon. friend was saying that Cominco made a profit during the years I referred to. Assuming the company made a profit, then I assume he is saying as well that they paid no taxes on that profit. Is that the standard of corporate behaviour that my Conservative colleague is recommending for Canada? Does he expect us to get down on our knees to corporations just because they provide employment?

Member reconcile the attitude of his Party in Question Period today on the textile issue, which is consistent with Shirley Carr and the CLC's position, with his Party's policies on external affairs dealing with the same issue? subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that my friend has failed to elaborate a contradiction. He has certainly left me, and I am sure most of those watching the debate today, completely baffled. We have been saying in our fiscal plan since 1984 that previous government policies, supported by his Party, produced an undue tax burden on individuals and far too little on corporations. This Budget addresses that concern. It moves us
one step closer to commercial corporations paying a fair share of tax.
I am absolutely astonished, given previous comments made by this Member of the House, that he has not read his own Party's policy documents relating to external affairs and the repercussions and implications for Canadian jobs of the position his Party is taking, specifically in the textile industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I want to make it clear that the Budget which the Government brought down, as thin as it was and as do-nothing a Budget as it was, still managed to raise taxes to ordinary Canadians. In fact, because of the trade deal the Government negotiated with the United States and because of the loss of roughly $500 million of tariff revenues, the Government had to raise sales taxes in the Budget.
The Government is placing greater and greater burdens on the backs of ordinary Canadians. Ordinary Canadians are saying that enough is enough. They want the Government to stop putting the burden on their backs and to develop a fair taxation system. They want the Government to stop letting its friends get off scott-free, to stop letting the large corporations which make millions of dollars of profit get off with paying no income tax.
Even President Ronald Reagan has had the courage to impose a minimum income tax on large corporations. Why can a Canadian Government not assure Canadians that profitable corporations will pay some tax and that all of the burden will not be put on the backs of ordinary Canadian families?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am standing in my place today to address certain issues which were omitted by the Minister of Finance in his Budget, more specifically with regard to the homeless and those who live in inadequate housing. I have risen on several occasions in this Flouse to remind the government that in 1987, the International Year of the Homeless, over 100 000 people have slept in the streets in this fine country of ours. This situation is unacceptable in a country as rich as Canada and one where winters are so harsh.
Since the right hon. leader of the official Opposition has made me housing critic, I have been monitoring the results of policies put forward by this government, mainly because this Government had promised so much before the 1984 election. I have before me, Mr. Speaker, the Government's campaign commitment as stated in the manual for Tory candidates entitled "Pocket Politics '84", with regard to those who are the most in need in our country. In the area of social programs, the Conservative Government promised assistance to Canadians who are unable to meet their own needs. The Government's intentions were made even more interesting by the fact that it announced at the same time a new orientation of its efforts in the area of housing, to assist the poorest and the neediest. According to the new policies announced in 1985, the Government regrouped planning activities at the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation under three different headings: market housing, social housing and housing assistance. Actually, the Government also used this opportunity to transfer to provinces the administration of some programs, under the pretext that program delivery would be improved.
We in the Liberal Party always have had reservations as to the wisdom of that move. Indeed, my colleague for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) always questioned the move, and rightly so. What the Government did is not simply an administrative decision to improve program delivery, but as we now realize, it abdicated its responsibility as a Federal Government to exercize leadership, and to determine criteria and policies in the face of problems of a national nature such as the homeless.
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
The Government also imposed budgetary cut back on the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to avoid what the Conservatives called wastage.
Before going any further, I would like to indicate it is the opinion of the Liberal Party that no further cuts should be made to the Corporation's operating budget. It is our view that any additional cut would jeopardize the Corporation's ability to fulfill its basic mandate.
This Budget is important also in that the Minister of Finance already informed the House of his intention to implement his famous tax reform. The reform's second stage could impact negatively on home building. New provisions for a yearly tax on land developers will lead to increased costs that will have to be borne by tenants and new home buyers. This is the view of a number of groups such as the Canadian Home Builders' Association who are concerned with that new tax, and more still by the way it will be implemented. At any rate, the Standing Committee on tax reform already has been made aware of that problem. This is an example of a counterproductive move by the Government.
This Budget is a clear statement that the Conservative vision of finance is loaded. Because we now see that the Government has not reached its goal of helping the most in need.
Let us pore over the results together. The International Year of Shelter for the Homeless was meant first to awaken us to that still serious problem in developing countries, but it had a boomerang effect in making us aware of the phenomenon in developed countries, Canada included, unfortunately. The Government's response, in 1987, was to organize studies and conferences on that phenomenon. That was done in September 1987. Six months later the Government has not yet solved the problem. It could at least show leadership and bring all parties around the same table, so they could acknowledge the report and make sure the federal Government will find someone to look after the homeless. The federal Government must take the lead and identify policies, responsibilities, the various levels of government and the necessary funding of various parties in that issue.
In the United States, two examples show that despite a budgetary deficit, it is still possible to put into place measures to solve the problem of the homeless. One example comes from the Government of the United States and the other from the State of Massachusetts. First, in the remarks of Congressman Lyndy Boggs before the National Social Service Conference of the American Salvation Army, we read the following, and I quote:
Federal level of response to homelessness has had an important and probably critical boost from the energetic urging of the new Speaker of the House of Representatives- representative Jim Wright of Texas. In the first days of the 100th Congress in January, he visited a shelter for homeless men in the District of Columbia, met with Mitch Snyder, the well known advocate for the homeless, and spoke out with urgency and compassion about the need to

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
act quickly in support of a bill that would provide $500 million for shelters and an additional measure providing emergency food aid.
The House passed that Bill, HR. 558, on March 5, 1987, by a vote of 264 to 121.

Everything is possible to those determined enough who also consider housing as a necessity of life. The Americans went even further. There is the following in that same speech, and I quote:

This Bill represents the fact that the federal government does have a moral and legal obligation to feed, clothe, and house homeless people who are in every community across this country both urban and rural.

That obligation does not seem to exist in Canada. There is more. The Chairman of the Banking Committee, Mr. St. Germain, added, and I quote:

-this is only a preliminary response and an emergency one at that. The failure of the Administration and the Congress to continue to provide the absolutely essential housing assistance to low and moderate income people has directly resulted in the homeless situation that we see in all our communities.

A few Tory Members must be thinking that this poor Liberal Member is making up stories and does not understand the need for deficit reduction. This same need for deficit reduction argument is also invoked in the United States. Fortunately for our neighbors South of the border, on the housing issue, good sense prevails, and we can understand that it is sometime necessary to forget about budgetary deficit when dealing with Canadian men and women who have no roofs over their heads.
Lyndy Boggs also stated:

The program cut-backs in recent years due to the federal budget deficit and policies of the current Administration have, I am afraid, contributed to the problem of homelessness. Other problems such as economic distress in certain parts of the country as well as widespread de-institutionalization of the mentally ill have also played a part in creating the problem we now face.
[ Translation]
Do you believe that the situation in Canada is quite different? It would be unwise to extrapolate and say: Such being the case in the United States, such must be the case also in Canada. There are several things in both countries which are different, including our social security systems which are quite superior to those in existence in the United States.
What should be emphasized here is the initiative taken by the House of Representatives which has clearly established the American administration's responsibility for homeless people in the United States, declaring at the same time: No matter the extent of our deficit, it is more important to provide a roof over the head of each American citizen.
The experience carried out in Massachussett is also quite convincing, because it demonstrates what can be done where there is a political will.
The Governor of that State had established a committee made up of people involved in providing shelters for the homeless to determine first how to provide emergency shelters to the homeless, and second how to develop strategies aimed at ensuring the social rehabilitation of the homeless in this New England State.
In the United States, there is, on the one hand, a federal administration which is faced with a huge deficit and, on the other, the State of Massachussett's Government which has no deficit at all. Both Government have decided to deal, together with the interested parties, with the problem of the homeless and to do so openly.
In Canada, during the International Year of the Shelter for the Homeless, various conferences were held, and funds for short term or emergency facilities were collected.
But if we do not address the long term problem, these measures will be nothing but band-aids which will not solve the problem. I am aware that it is difficult to address this problem, but nobody expects miracles. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) missed a fine opportunity to demonstrate to us that his Government has the political will to remedy the situation.
I do not question the need for the Government to reduce the deficit, but I feel there are items in the Budget which are more important than others, including the need for a home. The Government should behave like every ordinary citizen who makes cuts in his personal budget because of dicreased revenues. Such a citizen would reasonably cut such items as entertainment; he would put little or no money in his saving account; he would not change his car every year and would postpone his trip down South.
However, he would not forego the amounts needed for food, clothing and housing. He would not cut back on health care either since he has access to health insurance anywhere in Canada. He might cut back on food, find a less expensive appartment, pospone the purchase of luxury clothing items, but he would always make sure of having the strict minimum. But what does the Canadian Government do?
It says that, for all practical purposes, the budgetary deficit has to be brought down by all means available, and this includes ignoring the fact that 100 000 Canadians are homeless. The Government also ignores all the problems related to that fact.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is discriminating against the homeless. When our fellow citizens in Alberta were hit by a tornado and a few communities were razed to the ground, we immediately took action to help those who needed it the most.
1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, is there any difference between losing your home because of a tornado and losing it because of
February 22, 1988

a lay-off, family violence, a series of misfortunes or your inability to cope with them?
The result is the same: You find yourself without a home.
Why this lack of interest for the homeless? This issue is extremely important. There is no discrimination against the sick. If someone has spent his entire life smoking and having activities which were harmful to his health, will he be refused treatment because he was not careful? Of course not. When it comes to meeting basic needs, there can be no discrimination.
Yet, in its Budget, the Government hides behind budgetary cut-backs to justify what cannot be justified, its abandonment of poor Canadians whose only home is the street. They cannot even receive their welfare cheques as they do not have an address.
Mr. Speaker, is the Government as hard on itself as on the homeless? Apparently not. It applies a double standard. If we add everything up, we see the true face of this Government. If you add the $1.6 billion used to bail out the CCB and Northland Bank, the cost of the Estey Commission, the cost incurred in moving the jail to Port Cartier and, worst of all, the judicial expenses for the defence of a previous Regional Development Minister who keeps pretending he is innocent despite the evidence to the contrary, you readily realize that the Government is not working for the poor. On the contrary, the cuts made at the expense of the needy are used to finance the Government's gigantic blunders.
In fact, every social program in the housing area is under attack. Among the most striking needs is housing for the native peoples. In a press release commenting the last Budget, George Erasmus, head of the First Nations Assembly, stated that the non-statutary cuts of $300 million were geared to native people programs. These cuts did not affect the Defence nor the External Affairs budgets, which were exempted. Chief Erasmus took this opportunity to underline the fact that with a submarine costing $1 billion, the First Nations could build 16,333 houses, while creating 200,000 full time jobs on the reserves and house 68,000 persons there.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where do we place our priorities at a time of budget restraints? Is it to put a roof over the head of our fellow Canadians or to give us the luxury of a nuclear submarines fleet? I realize that while this comparison may look ridiculous to some of our colleagues, it points to the main question: Where are the true priorities of this Government that claims it wants to help those who need it most?
Now, who are the homeless? Who do we deprive of a roof over their head and of the possibility of reintegrating our society? They are mothers such as Mrs. Fleather Walker who was forced to place her two daughters with Toronto's Children Aid Society before going to the St-Michael Hospital to get psychiatric help. Mrs. Walker, a 30 years old woman who received no financial support from her husband, was living with her two little daughters in a 7 by 14 foot bachelor apartment. She was paying $400 a month for that bachelor
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
furnished only with a small desk, a chair and two small tables. The place was infested to such a point that cockroaches would crawl over the little girls' body while they were asleep at night on the floor. One can imagine the bad effect of such an environment on the health of those two children, one of which has now developed suicidal tendencies. Unable to afford a healthy home large enough for their needs and at an affordable rate, this family is now materially apart, mentally affected and on the verge of becoming homeless. And their story is one of the many paths to a homeless situation.
Let me remind the House that 22 percent of the homeless in Canada are women in a difficult situation. They are either old, head of a single parent family or sick. I would also point out that many homeless are persons with psychiatric problems who were released from institution for all sorts of good common sense administrative reasons which were to save us large amounts of money. But we only forgot one thing, that is to provide proper accommodations for them. Now they are left alone and distraught on the street.
Last Fall, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) talked about the case of a homeless woman who was attacked in the Jeanne-Mance Park in Montreal during the night, while sleeping. A few days later, she died as a result of her wounds.
Another example mentioned to the house by my colleague the Hon. Member for Bourassa was the case of Kenneth Ryan, 42 years old, who lived in Halifax and became homeless as a result of difficulties which he could not solve. He too was found dead early September, also victim of an attack apparently.
The homeless are at the mercy of everything. This is an aspect that we, Hon. Members, in the safety of our homes, cannot realize. Without fixed address, there is no welfare cheque, there are no walls to protect you from the wind, from the cold, from the rain or there is even less protection from individuals who will shamelessly rob you of the little you own.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) stressed in a statement he made in this House on September 15 last that 57 percent of the homeless in the province of Manitoba were natives.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) also mentioned the case of young homeless people. According to a study about young drifters in Montreal made in 1985, in the 18 to 30 age group, one in two had previously lived in a foster home or in an institution; 80.3 percent do not have any contacts with their families and are generally faced with two serious problems: alcohol and drug abuse as well as mental illnesses; 23 percent of those studied had already been hospitalized in psychiatric wards. There are many suicide attempts, and it is of course very difficult to keep a job in those conditions.
In an article published in the Mail Star, we learned of the plight of two teenagers without a home, Bill, 15 and Eric, 16.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Be Is her
They were fleeing from family problems and were lured by a possible job in a large center. We are told that Bill has not been sleeping for 36 hours and talks now with difficulty, which reveals extreme fatigue. Examples are numerous. All across the country, each case is more dramatic than the other.
Sometimes, government decisions have contributed to the problem, the renovation of popular neighbourhoods of Vancouver for Expo 1987 being a real example of that. Sometimes, people have had a hard life and could not or would not cope with it. In either case . . . Mr. Speaker, you are signalling me that my time is over. I will conclude momentarily-
There are, clearly, in the problem of the homeless, things that the federal Government can change. Flomeless people and those who help them are not expecting miracles and are not asking much. They want the Government to show leadership in the coordination of policies and solutions, in bringing together, at the same table, all the people involved with this problem. We have to start talking to one another.
It is important to allow all the participants- municipalities, provincial governments, voluntary agencies, the homeless themselves-to seek and find the problems that can be solved and to do it as quickly as possible, before they become even more serious than they already are.
On January 25, 1987, the Liberal Caucus had the privilege to hear Theodore Sorensen who, for 11 years, wrote the speeches of John F. Kennedy. During the last 30 years, Mr. Sorensen had the opportunity to meet most American and Canadian leaders. That night he was asked to elaborate on what is leadership in a free society. He said that to be a good leader you did not have to be a good manager anymore, but also that it was not enough to be at the top to be a leader. He said, and I quote:
[DOT]	< 1530)

Effective political leadership is not a science but an art, requiring not calculation but judgment, not accurate measurements but wise choices.

1 wonder, today, whether it is wise to ignore the problem of the homeless and I urge the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to think about that problem. 1 wonder why the homeless were ignored.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are discussing amendments that have been put forward by members of the New Democratic Party and the Official Opposition. The amendment put forward to the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the motion which is before
the House put by the Official Opposition, states that we have failed to put forward a credible plan to deal with the national debt. It also states that we have failed to specify a Canadian approach for dealing with the instabilities of the international monetary system. They regret this. 1 point out that this is part of their preamble.
The amendment put forward by the NDP condemns the Government for introducing a Budget that ignores the real economic needs of the country and for the elimination of costly tax breaks. Members of that Party state that the Government should be condemned for maintaining a policy of high interest rates begun by previous Liberal Governments and for failing to introduce a system of universal child care.
1 am very pleased to be able to speak in the House this afternoon. I welcome the opportunity to speak in support of the Budget recently tabled in the House by the Minister of Finance. This Budget clearly indicates that we are on the right track with regard to securing the economic renewal of Canada, a promise that was made in 1984 by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Members on this side of the House are proud of the statistics that prove that in three and a half years of solid fiscal management the Government has turned our economy around and has put Canada into the top spot among major industrialized countries in terms of economic growth and jobs. As Canadians, members of the Opposition should also welcome this news.
In our Agenda for Economic Renewal tabled in November of 1984 the Minister of Finance stated, "First, we must put our own fiscal house in order so that we can limit and ultimately reverse the massive build-up in public debt and the damaging impact this has on confidence and growth." It is obvious that we have followed through with this principle.
In the four years ending in 1984-85 the deficit rose steadily from $14.9 billion to $38.3 billion. This was an increase of 150 per cent in just three years. In contrast, in 1988-89, the budgetary deficit will have been reduced for the fourth consecutive year, declining to $28.9 billion. In 1989-90 the budgetary deficit will be down to $28.6 billion. Relative to the size of the economy, the deficit will have been cut in half over this five-year period. We are still not satisfied, however, with what the deficit is going to be. There is much work that has to be done.
Of equal significance is the number of jobs that have been created in Canada as a result of increased confidence in the economy. Since the election of 1984 more than 1.1 million jobs have come about, and the unemployment rate has dropped to 8.1 per cent, the lowest level since September, 1981.
In my Province of British Columbia five times as many jobs have been created in the 40 months since we were elected than were created in total between the 1980 and the 1984 elections. The facts are clear-the Canadian economy has not looked this healthy in years.
February 22, 1988

Continuing on this path, the Budget includes a $300 million reduction in non-statutory spending by government Departments beginning in 1989-90. This will allow the Government to lower the deficit mainly through the control of expenditures.
In the most recent report of the Auditor General, Kenneth Dye stated that there have been significant improvements made in financial controls. He stated that the Government now has systems and procedures that provide essential financial controls. With expenditures by our federal Government exceeding $100 billion a year, protecting the public purse demands that the correct amounts be paid out to the intended recipients at the right time, he said. "A decade ago the Auditor General could provide no such assurance that this was happening. Today, I can do so," he stated.
The Budget reviews the fact that the average annual rate of increase in program spending has been cut to 3.5 per cent, less than the rate of inflation. When this is compared with the four fiscal years ending in 1984-85, when government spending increased at an average annual rate of 14 per cent, it is evident that we are on the right track.
From international comparisons of deficits, debt and interest payments it can be seen that there has been extremely promising news in controlling our deficit, particularly when we compare our figures with those of other OECD countries. Relative to the other OECD countries Canada has undertaken substantial actions to reduce its deficit in the last three years. The improvement in Canada's total government structural balance since 1985 exceeds that of the other countries. Our total government deficit as a proportion of the Gross Domestic Product in 1987 remained above the average of the G-7 countries.
At the federal level of government Canada has made extensive progress in reducing the deficit to GDP ratio. By 1988 this ratio is expected to be roughly equal to the G-7 average, in comparison to 1985 when the ratio was over two percentage points higher in Canada.
The word is out and the news is good. Canada's position in the international economic sphere is dynamic and well respected. An advertisement in The Sunday Times of London stated, for example:
Toronto: The fifth largest stockmarket in the world. For years it has been closed to overseas investors, but now, in the post-Liberal era, it is opening up and changes in political and economic conditions are now combining to create some of the most exciting growth opportunities in the world.
The Government has worked vigorously for a new round of multilateral trade negotiations under the GATT. Our trade agreement with the United States is a major building block in strategy to continue to strengthen our competitive position. As our largest trading partner and with a population of over 250 million, as compared to ours of just over 25 million, it is evident that access to this market by our goods and services will boost our economy and help to create a tremendous number of jobs in many sectors of the economy.
The Budget-Mr. Belsher
Our NDP friends have said that we are not doing anything about child care. Nothing could be further from the truth. 1 might add that the amendments to the Income Tax Act are proposed to implement the taxation aspects of our Government's new policy on child care. The maximum child care expense deduction will be increased from $2,000 to $4,000 for each eligible child who is under seven at the end of the year or who has a severe and prolonged mental or physical impairment. In addition, the over-all maximum limit of $8,000 per taxpayer for child care expense deductions will be abolished.
With respect to the refundable child tax credits, as proposed in the tax reform, the maximum amount of this credit for 1988 is $559 per child. A new $200 supplement in respect of children six years and under for families with low and middle incomes, to recognize the contribution made by the parent who cares for the child at home, will be added to the refundable child tax credit, some $100 for the 1988 tax year and some $200 for subsequent years.
Prepayment of the refundable tax credit was limited to families whose net income did not exceed $15,000. Proposed amendments will increase this income level to a rate that is two-thirds of the threshold level. This means that for 1988 the threshold for basic credit is $24,090, and two-thirds of that is $16,060. Anyone earning less than this amount of net income will receive the payment. In other words, the level is being raised by $1,060.
For 1988 the prepayment will be $100, but in subsequent years the prepayment will include two-thirds of the $200 supplement. Also, in 1990 and thereafter the amount of the $200 supplement will be adjusted to reflect increases in the Consumer Price Index greater than three per cent.
When we look at child care strategy we see that we are committed to spending $5.4 billion over seven years. We estimate that this will create at least 200,000 new child care spaces.
The proposed Canada child care legislation is a new costsharing program with the provinces to create 200,000 new, quality child care spaces. It will provide cost sharing for both non-profit and commercial child care. We are proposing this legislation to facilitate and to promote rapid development in the non-profit sector. It will be cost-shared to the tune of 75 per cent federal and 25 per cent provincial.
Details of the federal-provincial financial arrangements will be negotiated with provincial and territorial Governments. The federal Government will work with the provinces to ensure the development and implementation of the necessary standards for quality in a jointly funded child care system.
Under the heading of new tax assistance to families with young children, over 1.3 million families with pre-school aged children will receive increased benefits through changes to the child tax credit or the child care expense deduction. For

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Belsher
families with receipted child care expenses there is an increased tax deduction of up to $4,000 per child for children six years and under or with special care needs. For low and middle-income families there is a phased-in $200 per year supplement to the child tax credit for children six and under. For children over six years the tax deduction stays the same at $2,000 per year. The limit of $8,000 on allowable deductions per family will be removed.
There also is a special initiatives fund in the child care strategy. There is an estimated $100 million to promote research and development in child care, for example, in rural communities and for special projects that should be tried out.
Why did the Government establish this child care strategy? It is because child care is a priority issue for the Government and for Canadians. The Government promised Canadians a comprehensive child care system that would meet the needs of our families.
Last year I sat on the Special Committee on Child Care which had a mandate to examine the issue of child care and provide the Government with an indication of the needs of Canadian families.
This strategy could lead to as many as 40,000 jobs in the child care field itself and offer substantial training opportunities for child care workers.
1 wish to take another few minutes to deal with cutting down loopholes in the tax system. 1 feel that the opposition Parties do the Canadian people a disservice when they fail to acknowledge the various things that have already been cut out. For instance, over the past three years a number of measures have been introduced to protect the integrity of personal and corporate tax systems. Some of those measures include the following.
The Government has put an end to the abuse of the scientific research tax credit, which cost the economy billions of dollars. The Government has eliminated tax shelters based on investments in yachts and recreational vehicles; eliminated the use of trusts to distribute investment income tax free; terminated the use of partnerships in corporate takeovers to increase tax deductions; introduced a minimum tax for high income individuals; and introduced measures which significantly restrict the ability of corporations to transfer losses and unused deductions.
There are still things that need to be done, but we are on the right track. Furthermore, the Government has said that there are income tax remission orders, but in an effort to enhance the accountability of those remission orders the Government has undertaken to do the following in the current fiscal year. It has undertaken to table in the House all income tax remission orders exceeding $20 million. The Government has also undertaken to provide periodic reports to Parliament of all orders and to publish all orders in the The Canada Gazette. This Government is not afraid to go to the people for accountability.
This afternoon it is my pleasure to say that I endorse what the Finance Minister has given to this House by way of his Budget address, and I deplore the two amendments put forward by the opposition Parties.

I wish to take this opportunity to ask a question of the Hon. Member. Quite a few times in his speech he stated that the Government is on the right track. He also mentioned that the Canadian economy has not looked healthier for years. We still have an annual deficit close to $30 billion. Our national debt is 60 per cent higher than it was in 1984. Every Minister of the Government stands up in the House and says, "We brought the interest rate down". That is good. It means that it costs us less to finance our national debt. However, why is that not reflected in the reduction of the annual deficit? Every expert, after February 10, agreed that if there had not been a change in accounting methods, the annual deficit would have been $32 billion, as it was on March 31, 1984, just before the election.
We have had economic recovery for six years, and the national debt has gone up by 60 per cent. The national deficit, taking into account what I call creative accounting-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Creative bookkeeping.

Could the Hon. Member tell the House what the Government did? I do not want him to say that they created jobs. Yes, they created jobs, but how many jobs did Canadians lose during that period of time? million. I mean, two and two make four. Could we have a more concrete explanation from the Hon. Member?
