subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in this place enough years and have been through enough Budgets to know that faces might change but the direction of Budgets and the priorities in them have not.
My colleagues and I have called this a Budget of lost opportunities. What would happen if one were to grant all the claims of the Government and to say that all its claims were accurate, appropriate, and everything else? What would happen if one were to say that, even though it stretches

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Benjamin
credulity? First we would have to take a look at what is happening in the economy across the country and at everything that needs to be done as a necessary investment on behalf of the people of the country and the country as a whole. We would also have to look at what has really happened over the last several years. We say that this is a Budget of lost opportunities because the Government has missed a golden chance to do that which needs to be done.
Everyone agrees that we need more employment and more revenues for the national Treasury. However, this administration and the previous one, at least in their last two years in office, were so hypnotized by the deficit that they proceeded to give it priority over anything else in the nation. They felt that a supreme effort had to be made to reduce the deficit.
We have been accused of being big spenders, debt loaders, and so forth. However, we must look at the history of my Party whenever it has been in government. We have always operated on the basis that every Government goes into debt most of the time, but we have always said-and we still say it-that a nation has different kinds of debts. There is constructive debt, what we have always called self-liquidating debt. There is destructive debt, what we call dead weight debt. Mr. Speaker, I would not want you to think for a moment, seeing as where you come from, that I am expounding some kind of Social Credit ideology. Far be it for me to say anything that would give credibility to that unlamented philosophy, but the fact of the matter is that when a nation goes into debt, the methods it uses to pay off those debts indicate its priorities.
Let us talk about the lost opportunities in the Budget. The Government had the opportunity to provide at least half a billion dollars a year more in housing of all kinds, even if it meant increased borrowings, which would have been constructive debt. As I have said repeatedly in the House over a number of years, in every city in the nation there is a waiting list as long as one's arm of people who need hospital beds, chronic care beds, and home care assistance. There are thousands of older homes of senior citizens that need fixing. There is a need for low income and co-operative housing. When one looks at housing, one realizes that it goes through the entire economy, all the way from the forest industry to the final forest products which are used in homes. It does not matter whether it is in the plumbing industry, the electrical industry or in all the other things that go into housing. The tens of thousands of people you put to work will start paying taxes. That is why we call it a self-liquidating debt. That kind of an investment-it is not a debt really but an investment- not only repays itself in a very short period of time, in two or three years, but it is a constructive kind of way to borrow and expend moneys on behalf of the nation as a whole.
In environment, we could put 100,000 young people to work starting yesterday with a few hundred million dollars a year just cleaning up our air and water. We have no right, none of us from any Party, as a nation to leave the kind of mess we are
leaving for others to clean up. The longer we take to clean it up, the more it will cost. Here is a constructive kind of debt not only to clean up the environment but which will put people to work who will pay taxes.
Let me come to municipal works. There are tens of thousands of needed necessary projects in the plans and desires of municipalities all over Canada, urban and rural. I do not mean luxury hotels and shopping centres; I mean necessary and needed public works, some of which are so dilapidated and worn out that they are becoming a disgrace in our communities. That is an investment, Mr. Speaker. It is not a loss or a straight out expenditure. Again, the federal authorities should be providing the leadership and getting the provinces to join in. A consortium of three levels of Government could put another
100,000	or 200,000 people to work who pay taxes, and the debt will liquidate itself. So much of our debt-as my hon. friend mentioned when he was speaking about the billions of dollars we have to put out just to service the present debt-is what 1 call a dead-weight debt, that is, moneys that are paid in interest charges.
In my own area of transportation, we need to invest $500 million to $1 billion per year over the next six or seven years. 1 think of urban transportation. I think of improvements to the St. Lawrence Seaway. 1 think of what is not happening and should be, and 1 think particularly about western Canada, but the same is true all over Canada in our railway industry. I was at a meeting of some 250 to 300 rural people, mostly farmers and their wives in Minton, Saskatchewan, a community in the riding of my good friend, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), who were fed up and angry about two railway branch lines that the Government has still not finished rehabilitating, even though those lines are guaranteed in the basic network to the year 2000. Some $11 million was spent a few years ago getting the job started, and another $14 million is needed to finish it. That puts a lot of people to work. It also lives up to a commitment by the Parliament of Canada, this Government and the previous Government, on railway branch lines in Canada, particularly in western Canada. In order for our railway operations to move faster and more efficiently, we have to deal with a mundane subject like the tens of thousands of level crossings where several hundred people get killed and a few thousand get injured each year. A few hundred millions of dollars in investment is needed there. It is an investment, not an expense. The fact that this Government and the previous Government have thrown hundreds of millions of dollars away, down the drain, refurbishing old worn out rolling stock for VIA Rail is terrible.
The Conservatives talk about bringing some sound business practices into Government. If you were to go to a banker and say, "I am going to start up this railway passenger corporation. 1 have no money. The youngest piece of equipment is 25 years old and some of it is 40 or 50 years old. I want some money to fix up the equipment and to operate a national passenger train service", every banker in this country would laugh you out of his office. But what does the Government do? It refuses to
February 22, 1988

order new equipment. Some of that equipment is to be refurbished for the third time since 1977. Talking about throwing good money after bad and talk about terrible business practices, that has to be it. I would not hire the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to run my chicken coop. If he calls that a sound business practice the way VIA Rail has been treated, then he does not deserve the portfolio of the Minister of Finance.
We have heard all the talk about employment and job creation and I have listened to government Members saying how many more jobs there are than there were four or five years ago. That is nice. But the Government would be in an even worse condition if that were not the case. Still, when you look at the whole country, unemployment in eight of the provinces is worse now than it was in 1984.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not. Be honest.

I think the Government and the Minister of Finance have to be reminded that there is more to Canada than Toronto and parts of southern Ontario. When you look at the different regions of this country, the provinces and the territories, and what has happened to unemployment in those areas, these fellows have nothing to brag about.
The other thing is that we need to lower the interest rate immediately by at least 1 per cent. As far as I am concerned, I don't particularly care what the value of the Canadian dollar is compared to the U.S. dollar. In fact, I hope the Canadian dollar goes down to 65 cents or 70 cents versus the U.S. dollar. I would follow the practices of Mr. Pearson and Mr. Diefen-baker. They slapped on foreign exchange controls, and hundreds of millions of dollars were not moving over the Canadian and United States border overnight for someone to make a fast buck on foreign exchange speculation. We had foreign exchange controls during the Second World War, the Korean War, in the middle 1950s, and in 1961, and we can have them again.

If the country is good enough to make a profit in, it is good enough to invest in. This running off to other parts of the world is not what I call good citizenship.
This brings me to another item. The Government needs more revenues to reduce the deficit. I will repeat for about the twelfth time that there is a good, neat way to get some revenue, would you believe, of at least $3 billion a year? The amount of deferred corporation taxes on the books of Canada now is approaching $40 billion, spelled with a "b" as in Benjamin dollars. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
It is an interest-free loan, and I do not know how other Canadians can get an interest-free loan when they want to buy a home, start up a business, or keep their farm going.
The theory was that if you allowed these corporations to defer taxes they would reinvest that money in fixing up their plant, increasing production and creating more jobs. Great theory. We started deferring corporate taxes in the early 1950s, I think, during the Korean War, and we got lots of investment. Look at International Nickel and Canadian Pacific. They invested all right. They invested in Guatemala, Australia, Indonesia, and lots of other places. Oh, yes! If the Government is so anxious about the deficit, this is an area where it can raise some revenue.
The whole thrust of this Budget, the philosophy behind it and of every Budget I have seen in this place, particularly over the last five years, and most particularly since 1984, is what I call the bottom line syndrome; the so-called market forces and free enterprise principles; the market-place should govern. All that has done, as far as I can see, is to appeal to greed, selfishness, and mediocrity. It is the philosophy, imported from south of the 49th parallel, of: What is in it for me? How many fast bucks can I make and the heck with everyone else. If I can make a buck, I do not care. That is the philosophy behind this Budget and the four others before it.

They talk about bringing business ethics to government. What these Tories have never learned is that you cannot bring business ethics into government. Look at all the trouble they got themselves into with their so-called business ethics. A lot of businesses have ethics they have not even used yet, especially the good ones. The ones they do use may not be illegal but they are the kind of ethics a back alley tomcat would use.
In a nation with all the needs I referred to earlier in housing, transportation, the environment, and municipal works, just those four areas alone, we still have tens of thousands of people lining up at food banks. When I was a kid they were called soup kitchens. Now some Tory wants to get up and tell me how great things are! Like R. B. Bennett and "prosperity is just around the corner". Really, it is a disgrace and a blot on this

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Benjamin
nation. Given the fact that tens of thousands of people are lining up at food banks and thousands of people do not have a home, we have no business sitting around here patting ourselves on the back, the Government or the Opposition. Let us get a fair tax system.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when he was Leader of the Opposition, said on television to my leader, talking about a fair tax system: "You're right, Ed". That is what he said. We are still waiting. We have a system so intrinsically unfair that it will allow tens of thousands of profitable corporations to avoid paying taxes, and that surely means some kind of political chicanery, free enterprise robbery, and a betrayal of our nationhood. They do not deserve that kind of treatment, that kind of unfairness and lack of integrity and honesty, which is the opposite of what they thought they were going to get when they elected the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 was most interested in the Hon. Member's comments, particularly with respect to the deficit and his feeling that more money should be spent rather than that an effort be made to reduce the deficit. I happen to have read an article in one of today's papers, The Toronto Star.

Mr. Donner has some interesting things to say and 1 would just like to read two or three of those comments and ask the Hon. Member a question.
First, Mr. Donner says that while most economists believe the Government should not need to balance its books in any particular year, nevertheless it should be able to do so over the longer term. He goes on to say that despite tax reform-and 1 think the Hon. Member was talking about a fairer system of taxes-Canada continues to have an extensive structural or non-cyclical deficit built into the system. That does not involve the question of putting people back to work and paying taxes and reducing the deficit. What that means is that there is just too much money being spent in relation to potential income.
Mr. Donner goes on and to say that the Canadian Government has gone about as far as it can go in controlling discretionary spending. If the structural deficit is to shrink further it will require additional taxes, perhaps via the soon-to-beintroduced national sales tax or via a reduction in transfer payments to provincial Governments or individuals. Nevertheless, he says, the structural or non-cyclical component of the deficit remains quite large. This issue will be on the political agenda of whatever Party wins the next federal election.
Bearing in mind that the Hon. Member seems to think his Party may very well win the next federal election-

speechtext: -I would like to ask him whether or not he truly believes that the way to reduce that structural deficit, which is going to be on the agenda of whatever Party forms the next Government, is either to call in all those deferred corporate taxes or else nationalize a bank in accordance with NDP policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member quotes a Mr. Donner. 1 never heard of him before.

speechtext: I am shocked. He is a well-known economist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The fact that he does so proves my case. He made reference to balancing the Budget over the longer term.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We agree with that. 1 want to recite a little bit of history for my hon. friend.
In Saskatchewan we took over a Government that was bankrupt from a Liberal administration and before that a Tory administration. It was absolutely bankrupt and had a debt which we were never going to be able to get out of. We increased the debt in the first four years of office from 1944 to 1948. We increased the debt and took electricity to 60,000 farms. We brought in hospitalization and medicare. We rebuilt the whole highway system. We built hospitals and schools. We borrowed the money. We cancelled the seed grain debts and the farm relief debts and we put the people of Saskatchewan to work. By 1952 we had balanced Budgets and we had balanced Budgets every year thereafter. That was a bankrupt province.
We will have to clean up that mess for the third time. The Liberals got back in in 1964 and we got back in in 1971. We had to clean that mess up again. Now the Tories got us in debt in spades in Saskatchewan to the tune of $2 billion.

February 22, 1988

five-cent-per-litre or twenty-three-cent-per-gallon tax increase on gasoline since 1984? Could the Member also comment on the tax on rural Canada which is also called the tax on long distance phone calls? In rural areas across Canada in order to phone the doctor, the farm machinery dealer and so on, one has to make long distance phone calls. Surely that is an area in which the provinces and municipalities need funding for roads, streets, and other things which they must build and maintain. 1 would personally rather see an export tax on the export of energy resources from Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

That has been sold out as well, but that would seem to me a proper place. They are our resources that are worth so much to us. That is an area in which revenue could be picked up.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when you were a boy did your mother ever give you advice? I will bet she did, Mr. Speaker. My mother used to give me advice too.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not enough.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I was a boy she used to give me advice, and even later on she used to give me a lot of advice. I always listened carefully to what she had to say. I do not know what
The Budget-Mr. Redway
sort of advice your mother gave you when you were a boy, Mr. Speaker, but I will never forget one of the things that my mother said to me. She said that I should never, never accept the job of Finance Minister of Canada if it were ever offered to me.
She said that because she honestly believed that if I became the Finance Minister of this country I would be very much disliked. Actually, she used a somewhat stronger word than that and that is because that is the way she felt about it, as did her friends and most other people.
She was not talking, of course, about our present Finance Minister. She was thinking of some of the former ones such as Mr. J. L. Ilsley, Mr. Douglas Abbott, and Mr. Walter Harris, who in our household was known as "Six-buck Harris". Those are the sorts of Finance Ministers about whom my mother was thinking when she gave me that advice. She was not thinking about the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) because she did not know him. She passed away before he became the Minister of Finance.
It is interesting that, in spite of those comments which my mother made to me, which have always stuck in my mind, the present Minister of Finance seems to hold a great deal of respect in this country, unlike so many of his predecessors. That is in spite of the fact that he has now been the Minister of Finance for three and a half years. As you will recall, he brought down an Economic Statement in November, 1984. He brought down a Budget in February, 1985, a Budget in February, 1986, another Budget in February, 1987, and a Budget in this year, 1988. That is four Budgets by my arithmetic. There has been the Economic Statement and four Budgets. On top of that he brought out a White Paper on tax reform and an actual tax reform package.
Normally that sort of thing done by one person in the job of Finance Minister would get a lot of people upset. With all those shots that he has had at the taxpayers of Canada, if my mother's advice was correct, just about everyone in this country would be hopping up and down mad at our Finance Minister by this time. However, that is not the case. In spite of all that, he is still a very highly respected person. Daily we read fine comments about him by all sorts of commentators. As a matter of fact, just over the noon hour my French teacher had me read some passages from the Quebec press, en francais, and some fine things were said about our Minister of Finance. That suggests to me that there is something different about the present Minister of Finance from the kinds of Finance Ministers we have had in the past.
That is also quite surprising when one considers the problems that faced the Minister of Finance when he came into office. He had to deal with an economic situation in September, 1984, in which unemployment was extremely high.
I recall the time when I was campaigning during and before the 1984 election, knocking virtually on every door in my

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Redway
constituency. If there was one thing that struck me more than anything else, it was that virtually everyone at every door 1 knocked was touched in some way by unemployment. There was either someone in the household itself who was unemployed, or a relative, neighbour or friend who was unemployed. Virtually everyone to whom 1 spoke when I campaigned throughout 1983 and 1984, was touched by the economic recession which was its worst since the Great Depression of the 1930s.
Since September, 1984, there has been a very substantial change. 1 need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the unemployment rate across the country has fallen very substantially, from some 12 per cent down to 8.1 per cent. While I am concerned about the economic situation in Canada as a whole, I suppose it is quite natural that I be more concerned about my constituency where we have gone from a dreadful unemployment situation which approached that of the Great Depression to a condition of virtual full employment. The unemployment rate in my constituency in Metro Toronto is around 4 per cent and perhaps lower. Traditionally, economists have said that an unemployment rate of around that figure is virtually full employment, because there are always people who change jobs no matter how good the economic times.
That situation of virtual full employment in my constituency in Metropolitan Toronto is quite evident when one visits any of the businesses or looks in any of the store windows. Inevitably one finds help wanted signs in those businesses or sees help wanted advertisements in the papers throughout the area.
1 do not suggest for a moment that this is a general condition across Canada, but it is a very substantial step forward and one for which I think the Government can take an enormous amount of credit.
This situation has not developed as a result of the Government creating jobs in itself. It has been brought about by the creation of a climate in which the private sector can create those jobs. In his address the Minister touched on a number of reasons why the private sector has been able to create those jobs. He referred to the deregulation that has taken place in energy, transportation, and financial services. He referred to the new Competition Act, modernizing our combines investigation laws that had not really been dramatically changed for some 20 or 30 years. The Government brought in the new competition laws, which again helped to set the climate for creating jobs and bringing about that dramatic change in the unemployment situation.
In addition, there has been privatization of many of the Crown corporations and undertakings. During the weekend we heard about problems in Manitoba where the Crown corporation administering automobile insurance has been accused of not operating fairly or properly. People are saying that this proves that Governments really should get out of the business of being in business and should leave that to the private sector. If that is the case under an NDP Government in Manitoba, it
makes sense that the privatization that has taken place so far has also helped stimulate the economy.
Another area which has helped to set the climate for an improved economic situation is the change in investment policy through Investment Canada. We are looking forward to the tax reform package that the Minister of Finance presented to the House a few months ago. That is one aspect of the economic situation that has changed dramatically as a result of the policies of the Government and the Minister of Finance.
Inflation is another consideration. Prior to the 1984 election there was galloping inflation. During my days of municipal Government at that time, inflation was rising dramatically. I recall that we had to contemplate paying inflation bonuses to our employees to make up for that inflationary rate because we knew that they could not afford to exist on the wage rates they were being paid before that inflationary rate suddenly started to take off.
I recall that when we wanted to give an inflationary bonus to unionized workers in our municipality there was a great problem with management just giving that inflationary bonus without actually negotiating with the union. The unions were upset that management should be giving a raise to their members without actually having had a say in that as well. This is what happened prior to 1984 during that dramatic period of wildly escalating inflation.
The situation has changed since the Government has been in office. While inflation certainly has not disappeared, it has become stable, at a greatly lower rate compared to what it was in the years prior to 1984. We now have the promise of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement which will help to hold down prices and the inflation rate. For the first time a federal Government is implementing a positive policy that will deal with inflation and help to hold down prices. This is something for which people on fixed incomes have been crying for years.
I constantly receive calls and letters from senior citizens in my constituency complaining about even a modest increase in the inflationary rate we have now as compared to that in the early 1980s. I get these letters and complaints all the time. Now for the first time we have a Government which is taking some positive initiative to counteract that inflation rate through the free trade agreement.
We have heard in the House this afternoon about what the deficit situation was like prior to 1984. We know that when the Government took office, between everything the Government took in in the way of revenue and everything the Government paid out in the way of expenditures, there was a shortfall of almost $40 billion. As my colleague in the NDP said, that is "billion" spelled with a "b". That is a lot of money. That deficit has not been eliminated. No one is suggesting that for a moment, but the annual spending deficit is now at least $10 billion less than when the Government took office.
February 22, 1988

You and 1 know, Mr. Speaker, how hard it is to cut back on our own expenditures and to balance our own books when they get out of whack. We know very well that it ain't easy to cut back expenditures by $10 billion.
If we had continued with the economic policies we had prior to 1984, we would be in a state, as we were prior to 1984, of economic chaos. Many people ask what that has to do with the Government. Times are relatively good now. Things have improved, unemployment is down, inflation is down and the deficit is down. What does that have to do with the present Government?
People who ask that question, including the Leader of the Official Opposition and the Leader of the NDP, are the people who say: "Look, this is just a world trend we are following here, Canada is just tagging along on the coattails of everyone else. The Government has not done anything to create the situation, it has all happened on its own". However, you and 1 know, Mr. Speaker, that every single economic indicator in Canada shows that Canada is the leading industrial nation now. Our economy is the leading economy in the industrialized world. We are not following anyone. In fact, we are dragging everyone else along. We are the leaders. Some of that has to be due to the policies of the Government and of the Minister of Finance, and I think it is quite clear that that is the case.
Having said all that, one would wonder if I had not been trying to prove that my mother was wrong when she said that everyone dislikes Ministers of Finance and one should never be a Minister of Finance. On occasion we all hear people saying that we would be better off if we did not have some of the policies that had been followed during the last three and a half years. For instance, we have heard senior citizens say that they should have more money in their pockets, their pensions should be bigger and the economic policies that have been followed have had a bad effect on senior citizens. I was thinking about that too, and I just wondered what has happened to senior citizens over the last three and a half years. 1 wondered whether or not the Minister of Finance has been awfully tough on senior citizens.
I am not saying that all senior citizens are doing well, but when I thought about it, 1 thought, first, that the Old Age Security, the one that starts at age 65-you are a long way from that, Mr. Speaker, and you will not qualify for that for a long time-continues to be fully indexed. That has increased every year since the Government has been in office. Senior citizens who are receiving Old Age Security benefits certainly have more money in their pockets now than they had back in 1984.
Then I thought of the Guaranteed Income Supplement. That is the one that provides for those who have no income or limited incomes, and that too continues to be fully indexed. All of those senior citizens who receive Guaranteed Income Supplement payments are receiving more money now than they were in 1984.
The Budget-Mr. Redway
Then I thought of the spouse's allowance, the one that is geared to income. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Government introduced an extension of the spouse's allowance. On top of that, there were improved benefits under the Canada Pension Plan, improved benefits under the Canada Assistance Plan, increases in the New Horizons grants, new senior citizens housing, particularly in my riding, and new benefits for veterans and for veterans' widows.
When 1 look at all of those things, I have to think that although I believe my mother has always been right, if she looked at the performance of this Government and of the Minister of Finance today, I think she would have to admit as well that the record has not been too bad at all, in spite of the fact that this has been a period of restraint.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest, as I usually do, to the comments of the Hon. Member. His comments are usually entertaining and I often find myself agreeing with his kind of easy going way of putting forward the facts. However, I was following his comments very closely today and I must admit that I detected what I considered to be several factual errors in his presentation, errors which 1 feel ought to be pointed out to the Hon. Member. I think he ought to have the opportunity to-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you saying his mother wasn't right?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps his mother wasn't right, that's correct. There were several factual errors in his presentation which I feel duty bound to present to the Hon. Member and ask him to reflect upon.
First, I recall that he said that prior to the 1984 election, Canada had experienced a period of galloping inflation. I think the Hon. Member would probably agree with me that that statement really requires a bit of qualification. I do not think it is entirely correct to say that just prior to the 1984 election, which is perhaps what the Hon. Member was implying, we had experienced a period of galloping inflation. It is true that in 1981 and 1982, Canada, like many other countries in the world, had experienced a period of galloping inflation. We had to raise interest rates in Canada to very high levels and, again, this was not something that was particular to Canada but it was common to many countries in the OECD, the United States, Great Britain, France, West Germany and the like.
In 1982 or 1983, the previous Government introduced the policy known as the six and five policy. Its goal was the reduction of inflation to 6 per cent in the first year of the policy and 5 per cent in the second year. As I recall, and I would put it to the Hon. Member, those targets were not only met but were exceeded to the point that in 1984, the rate of inflation, for probably the first eight or nine months of the year prior to the current Government taking office, had come down to below 5 per cent. I think it was four per cent or something in that neighborhood, if I am not mistaken.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
A second error, if I may call it that, in the Hon. Member's presentation was when he referred to the fact that every single economic indicator shows that we are among the leaders. It is true that Canada's economy has performed very well in the past several years. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his speech indicated that we were in the sixth year of an economic recovery period. That in itself indicates that the recovery began prior to the present Government taking office. But one indicator which the Minister did not refer to in his speech was the indicator that is known as the percentage of the GROSS National Product spent on research and development. It is sometimes referred to as the GERD to GNP ratio. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) is in the House. Perhaps he could add a few words to this debate.
The GERD to GNP ratio, or the gross expenditures on research and development as a percentage of GNP, has come down in Canada since the last election. We are moving up toward the target that had been set by the previous Government of 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product. Again, the figures from Statistics Canada indicate that since the last election this indicator has dropped to approximately 1.3 per cent. It was getting close to about 1.4 per cent prior to the last election. I suggest to the Hon. Member that these are several areas in which he might wish to qualify, perhaps, the statements that he made during his presentation.
To conclude I would like to say that what we are probably seeing is a situation in which, superficially, our country is basking in a period of economic growth. I ask myself serious questions about what kind of a country we are preparing for our children and our grandchildren 10, 15 or 20 years down the road if we are not taking steps to invest in research and development which will provide us with the kind of competitive economy that we need to compete in a global market.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments and the questions of my hon. friend. I have to say that my mother lived through the Great Depression. One thing that she knew about was a devastated economy. If there was one lasting impression that she conveyed to me it was those impressions of a devastated economy during the 1930s.
The Hon. Member talked about the inflation rate and the unemployment situation prior to the 1984 election. He talked about how the former Government dealt with inflation. He is quite right, that Government certainly did deal with inflation. It dealt with it in such a way that it raised interest rates to 20 per cent or more. It bankrupted an enormous number of companies. The result of that was massive unemployment. It is this unemployment from which we are still struggling to recover.
The message that I have been trying to get across is the message that my mother conveyed to me. I wish to convey that message from her to you, Mr. Speaker, and to other Members of the House. This sort of thing is unacceptable. We need a
Government and a Minister of Finance who know how to manage the economy properly. If there is one thing that can be said about the last three and a half years it is that the Minister of Finance and the Government have been doing just that, managing the economy properly. Thus we do not have either skyrocketing inflation or great depths of unemployment. What we have is a balanced and stable rate of inflation. We have a growing employment situation. That is good economic management.
You seem to be giving me the message, Mr. Speaker, that I should wind up my remarks. I would like to comment further on the other part of the Hon. Member's question. If you would like to recognize me after the next speaker has finished, Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to respond then.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret that the Hon. Member's time has expired. The time allotted for questions and comments has now terminated. The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) on debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to rise today to speak to the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) which he tabled on February 10. I must say that if Canadians are wondering what this Budget does for them as individuals and as families they will have to look long and hard. It is not surprising that the only measure that comes quickly to mind is yet another tax increase by the Government. This time I refer to the 1 cent per litre on gasoline to take another $300 million out of our pockets. I am sure that this increase bothers most Canadians as it bothers me when we go to fill up our tanks. The Budget will no doubt be remembered in history as a do-nothing Budget, although being able to refer to it as the last Conservative do-nothing Budget is somewhat comforting. No matter what one calls it the truth remains that despite the many significant challenges facing Canada the Minister of Finance had surprisingly little hesitation to say on budget day that Conservative policies and initiatives have worked and that holding the course was his plan of action as though there was nothing at all that he and his colleagues needed to do. Unfortunately, this is the wrong view of what is happening out in the real Canada. The Conservatives seem to be looking out of a rose-coloured window pane. I suggest most of it is centred on central Canada. They fail to see the numerous challenges facing us as a nation. The Government would do well to open the window and to peer out across the land to see what is really happening.
I put forth a challenge to the Government here today. I challenge it to do some checking and to take note of the many needs facing the country instead of sitting back with that everything-is-fine attitude it demonstrated so clearly in the Budget, proposing no new action plans to help those who need help, including relief and housing needs for low income families, displaced workers, illiterates or people in need of job skills retraining. I do not know where the Government went or
February 22, 1988

with whom it consulted to discover that on budget day all it had to do was stay the course.
However, I put it to the Minister of Finance that his Budget was inadequate. Staying the course is not good enough for Canadians. Just buying nuclear submarines certainly will not answer the needs that we see in our society. Canadians expected more from their Government, more than mere attempts at cutting the deficit to please Bay Street, while placing the burden of the deficit battle on the backs of families and middle-income earners. Canadians have a right to better treatment than that.
One of the few actions the Government did take in the Budget was the writing of its own report card. However, as one would expect from a youngster permitted to write his or her own report card, he or she would probably tend to stretch the truth, play up the good news and downplay the bad news. In the same way I am afraid that the Minister of Finance has fallen victim to the same type of trap.
For example, the Government was quick to take credit for a fairly healthy economy, yet it failed to take notice of, or to take the blame for, the unequal distribution of the economic upturn among the different regions of the country. We still have widespread unemployment. The 1.1 million people who are unemployed are concerned, as are those who are underemployed.
The Budget also went to great lengths to paint a rosy economic future for Canada but, alas, in the days since the Minister of Finance put his brush to the canvas to paint this rosy scenario and take credit for having created it Canadians have seen a far different picture. Representatives from some of the nation's largest and most respected financial institutions have expressed serious misgivings about the Government's dreamy economic scenario.
As 1 mentioned earlier, the Budget contains the Conservative's pursuit of a lower deficit by placing an increased burden on individual taxpayers and families while thousands of corporations pay little or no tax whatsoever.
The Tory attempts at cutting the deficit on the backs of Canadians began not long after they came to power. 1 am sure that we all remember well the summer of 1985 when seniors were forced to descend upon Parliament Hill and confront the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about his plans to remove inflation protection from their pensions. I would say that there is one rosy view that we can all take from that, and that is the fact that "grey power" is now in, and it is to the peril of any Government if it does not listen. From that point of view there is a rosy picture for all of us who are approaching those senior years.
An attack on income security for seniors, that is how the Conservatives have taken up the challenge of fighting the deficit, by showing complete disregard for the type of income
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
security for seniors that a nation such as Canada, with all its wealth, has long held to be a basic tenet of our social fabric. Those seniors who have been planning and preparing for their retirement years in order that they can live all of their lives in comfort as planned were damaged by the Government.
It was no surprise that seniors reacted strongly to this early item on the Tory agenda. It came out of nowhere, and fortunately it was beaten back. Yet it stands to this day as a symbol of the Government's lack of sensitivity and compassion for Canadians at all points on the income ladder.
Since coming into office the Tories have hit Canadians with dozens of new taxes. It reminds me of something that Adam Smith said which reflects the Tory view of who should shoulder the tax burden in this country. Adam Smith concluded that, "There is no art which one Government sooner learns of another than that of draining money from the people". Draining money from the people, how about that for a Conservative epitaph!
The facts speak for themselves. Today individual Canadians pay a greater share of the total tax bill in this country than they did when the Conservatives came into office, while corporations pay an even smaller share of the bill. It's that simple; it's that unfair.
Unlike its campaign promise not to raise taxes, the Government has seen fit to hit Canadians with more than $22 billion in new taxes, and then claim that it was its own ingenious management of Government that led to a lower deficit.
Let us take a look at the tax bill that the Tories have sent to Canadians since they came into office. It began with three consecutive increases in the sales tax. Starting from the word "go" in October, 1984, probably even before the first set of Ministers had found their offices, the Conservatives hit Canadians with their first tax bite which would, with subsequent increases, take another $3 billion from Canadians.
The Tories have extended the tax on candy, soft drinks and snacks. The cost to Canadians is $460 million. To this, one can add another $60 million for increased paint and wallpaper tax. Imagine what this tax did to the redecorating bills at 24 Sussex! This adds up to another $0.5 billion out of the pockets of Canadians.
As we were reminded in the latest Budget, there have been the Tory taxes on gasoline. There have been three increases here as well, one for $900 million, another for $450 million, and one more for $450 million. As if that were not enough, there was another increase of $300 million in the latest Budget. The grand total for the tax on driving, the gasoline tax, is $2.1 billion.
At least another $700 million was taken by the Government by increasing taxes on alcohol and tobacco.
Then there is the tax on talking, which came quietly into effect on January 1, 1988. Long distance telephone charges are

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
now subject to a 10 per cent tax. The cost to Canadians is $945 million.
Let us not forget the tax changes either, Mr. Speaker. Canadians have not been able to forget the deindexing of the whole tax system. The bill for that is $635 million. Killing the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, which had helped so many young Canadian families get their start, was at a cost of $105 million to those families.
Temporary income surtaxes earned the Government $1.7 billion. A change in the tax treatment of dividend income earned the Government another $300 million.
These taxes that I have mentioned are only a sprinkling of the dozens of tax grabs by the Government, which total more than $22 billion from average Canadians, individuals, families, and seniors.
I feel that once again 1 should mention these tax grabs alongside the fact that so many thousands of corporations in this country are still paying no tax. It does not take long to see who the friends of this Government truly are.
If it is true that Canadians often vote from their pocket books, they will surely remember how the Government has treated them the next time that they go to the polls. If they do not, they might get what they deserve.
So far I have spoken only about the taxes that the Government has introduced. What we do not have the numbers on as yet are the costs to taxpayers of one of the worst of the Tory tax proposals, a tax on food. In my view, the idea symbolizes the cold-hearted Conservative view of Canada that nothing is sacred in the deficit battle, not even food. That can be divided between the edibles and the inedibles, and I still think that it is reprehensible.
The tax on food met with significant opposition from many sectors of our society because of its regressiveness. This tax would cost the same to a $200,000 a year person, for example, the bank president we heard so much about from the Prime Minister as it would to a senior on a fixed income, or a single parent family. The idea is ludicrous. What were the Conservatives thinking about when they came up with that particular tax?
Fortunately, the Government did see the light and it rejected the idea outright. It took an awful lot of reading into the record here in the House, and a lot of noise outside for the Conservatives to be sensitized to this inhuman approach. With its mere suggestion of a tax on food the Government demonstrated its insensitivity to the needs of Canadians across the income spectrum.
It has taken a good deal of time to sample the Government's record of increasing taxes on Canadians. From the pockets of hard working Canadians more than $22 billion has been taken by the Minister of Finance. On February 10 the same Minister stood in his place and told the House that all the Government needed to do was to "stay the course". That does not sound to
me like a plan of action. Staying the course certainly will not help the 3.7 million Canadians who are living below the poverty line in this country, nor will it bring any comfort to the
851,000	families existing below the poverty line. The suggestion of staying the course and offering no plan of action is an affront to the many Canadians who have a right to look to the Government for leadership. I am truly saddened by the Government's inadequate response to the despair being experienced in this country. I suggest again that the Government wake up to the reality of the difficult situations in which so many Canadians find themselves.
The Government has, with little hesitation, drained billions of dollars from the pockets of Canadians. Yet after 3.5 years in office it found it in itself to deliver a do-nothing, stay-the-course Budget with no new initiatives or measures to assist the needy who are among us.
While on the subject of taxes, I would like to take this opportunity to address the Government's tax reform package. If we drop all the optics, we know that Canadians have yet to see the whole tax reform package. Some would say that what we have seen so far is the good news on tax reform, although I would argue that one has yet to see the bad news side, the national sales tax. What we have seen so far is the Minister of Finance offering to return to Canadians $5 billion over the next five years under his tax reform plan. What Canadians will remember is the $22 billion that the Government has already taken. In my books a reprieve of $5 billion on an increase of $22 billion sounds an awful lot like a tax grab and not a tax reform.
1 would like to suggest that there exists a real world out there, the challenge facing many Canadians and challenges that the Finance Minister saw no need to address in this Budget. I am sad to say that we have been treated with a cavalier indifference since the Conservatives came into office. Poverty is at the heart of most of our social problems in Canada: ill health, crime, poor housing conditions, and family violence. The Government cannot continue to say that the poverty gap will be closed as economic conditions improve. The "trickle down" theory of economic growth simply does not work in the world in which we live. I would add that, when we speak of the poor in Canada, we are not referring to the unemployed alone. Indeed, we must also consider the working poor to be part of this category. It remains a fact that well over half of Canada's poor families do earn an income.
We need a program to address the serious needs of the working poor, a program of income supplementation for families who were hit hardest in the Government's 1985 Budget and tax reform package by the deindexing of family allowances, the reduction of the threshold level at which parents become eligible for the child tax credit, and the slashing of the child exemption.
February 22, 1988

This do-nothing Budget also marks the passing of another missed opportunity for the Government to introduce its long promised older workers' adjustment program. It has been two years since the previous labour adjustment benefits expired. With each passing day we have displaced workers facing growing despair. Many of them are unfortunately falling into the discouraged worker category of people who have given up looking for jobs because they believe none are available. The 1.2 million figure for unemployed people is certainly not a true reflection of all those who are unemployed. I call upon the Minister of Finance to go back to the drawing-board and find the missing pieces of his Budget, the ones that will address the problems of the chronically unemployed.
We need a strategy in Canada which incorporates job skill training, income supplementation, and tax credits, all tied to job creation. The Government has failed to fulfil the leadership role Canadians had every right to expect. It demonstrated this failure no more clearly than in the Budget of February 10.
The Minister failed to address a very significant area in his Budget. Since the Conservatives took office in 1984, the youth of the nation has been sadly neglected. This is unacceptable, for we all know that our young people are our most valuable resource. It is an undeniable truth that expenditures on their behalf are investments in the future not only of our young people but of our nation. Despite a huge influx of young people into the job market, the Conservatives have slashed and cut when it comes to programs aimed at giving them a boost.
Cuts to Challenge programs stand as a symbol of the Government's inattention to the needs of our youth. In 1985, $3 million was cut from the program, leaving a $205 million allocation. This is a lot of money, but obviously the program had come to be considered very worth-while. However, the very next year, 1986, there was an additional $17 million cut to $186 million. By 1988 we had seen plans to cut it back another $6 million to $180 million. The real irony is that in all the time since the Conservatives came into office the demand for this kind of youth program has only increased.
What is worse is that the cuts to the Challenge programs are but one example of the low priority the Government has placed in the future of our young people. I could give other examples, such as the 1985 freeze of the Canada Student Loans Program and a cut of $5 million; the cancelling of the Young Workers Exchange Program and a cut of $3 million; and the 29 per cent cut in the funding of on-campus Canada Employment Centres for students to $4 million to which soon to be graduates and summer students look for help and information about where to find jobs.
What is completely incomprehensible is that we have not likely seen the end of bad news for youth programs, for indeed one of the few commitments of the Minister of Finance in his Budget was a further $300 million cut from programs. We have yet to see where they will hit but, if the record shows us anything, youth programs are certainly not safe from the Conservative wield of the axe. These youth cuts symbolize in a
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
straightforward manner the Government's unwillingness to help directly our youth get off to a strong start. Its attitude seems to be: let the market-place take care of that. I say again that that is just not good enough for Canadians, not only young Canadians but every Canadian who wants to see our youth develop.
One thing included in the Budget was the Government's detailed plans for a national child care program. We in the Official Opposition fully support the fundamental idea, that is, the provision of more child care spaces for Canadians across the country. However, there is a great deal of concern among experts in the field of child care that the Conservative child care proposals will actually result in less money going to child care over the next seven years than would have been available had the Tories taken no action at all. They argue that what the Government has labelled as an increased commitment to child care is in fact a hidden long-term capping of child care expenditures. To be honest, they have called it much worse, but I need not repeat those kinds of words in this place.
These concerns may very well reveal that the Tories have found their perfect public policy-package initiatives that actually cut program spending but find a way to gift wrap the package in grandiose style and try to make it look like an increased commitment.
In participating here today in the budget debate, I cannot help but wonder what Canadians are thinking about the Government, a Government that swept into office in 1984 promising not to raise taxes but has overseen the largest tax grab Canadians have ever known. I hope Canadians will remember that the present Minister said on behalf of his Party, while sitting on this side of the House, that they would cut spending and not raise taxes, that tax levels in Canada were already too high. The Prime Minister repeated those promises soon after the 1984 election. I am sure Canadians are wondering where all this good will has gone and what has happened to the promises. These words and promises are coming back to haunt the Conservatives, and well they should. Canadians will not soon forget the Government going back on its word, and its failure to live up to the commitments it made before the election.
I take this opportunity to point out today that many Canadians are feeling a sense of unease and frustration about the Government's record, a record which will establish the Government in history for its failure to show strong, credible leadership on the many challenges facing us as a nation. Nothing was clearer than when the Minister stood and said: "We will stay the course".
It is appalling that a modern Canadian Government, after three and a half years in office, taxing Canadians more than they had ever been taxed before and fighting the deficit on the backs of families and middle-income Canadians, can come forward with a Budget with no pledge of action for addressing priorities such as the income gap between the rich and the poor and regional disparities.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Daubney
1 suggest that there are real challenges out there, and it is too bad the Minister's Budget has not dealt with them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate this afternoon on a Budget which demonstrates that the long-term plan laid down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November, 1984 is working. His policies were right then and the Government's policies are right now.
In 1984, the Government brought to office a vision for a stronger, more prosperous Canada now and into the next century, a vision that was rooted in our belief in Canadians themselves, their capacity to innovate and produce, their desire to excel, and their determination to build greater opportunities for the future. To make this vision a reality, we set out our agenda for economic renewal to transform the economy so that it could meet the challenges of a more competitive world. We have put in place a wide ranging series of actions that complement one another. We have revitalized the private sector and positioned Canada's economy to meet the challenges of international competition in the 1990s and beyond. We have restored fiscal responsibility by reducing the deficit and cutting the growth of the national debt. We have implemented priority programs and we have helped regions and sectors hurt by unexpected developments in the world economy.
The driving force behind productive growth and job creation is a dynamic private sector. To encourage this dynamism, the Government has taken far-reaching measures to modernize the regulatory environment for business. We deregulated the energy and transportation sectors. We opened financial markets to global opportunities and stimulated greater competition in financial services. We have modernized our competition policy, our copyright and patent legislation, providing better protection for the public interest. We also privatized some Crown corporations where it was clear that public ownership of part of the market-place was no longer justifiable or necessary. We created Investment Canada to encourage and welcome investment capital from abroad and to keep Canadian investment capital here, investment that is creating jobs for Canadians.
The Government has also taken far-reaching measures to reform the federal tax system. We are making the tax system fairer for individual Canadians and we are making it more effective in supporting growth and job creation. We are creating a system that helps our businesses and industries to compete in the world. On January 1 our reforms to the personal and corporate income tax systems went into effect. The key to these reforms is our belief that lower tax rates are the best possible tax incentives for productive activity. For individuals, three federal tax brackets are replacing ten. To make the system fairer we are converting personal exemptions and many deductions to tax credits. We are reducing and
February 22, 1988

eliminating many special tax breaks that permit upper income earners to avoid paying their fair share. The results are compelling. More than eight out of 10 households will see their personal income tax reduced. About 850,000 lower income Canadians will have their income tax reduced to zero. Almost nine out of 10 Canadians aged 65 and over will have income tax reductions. The vast majority of families with children will pay noticeably less personal income tax. For the corporate sector, many special tax breaks are being eliminated or reduced to permit lower tax rates. This will mean that the corporate tax system will be more competitive with systems in other countries. There is much more to be done, Mr. Speaker, and we will replace an archaic federal tax system with a new system that will be effective in supporting growth and job creation.
We have been working with the provinces and others to develop the most effective means of implementing this new system, particularly the opportunity to have an integrated national sales tax. So far, our progress with the provinces has been encouraging, but we have more work to do.
Another key element of our strategy for the 1990s is to secure improved access to world markets for Canada's exporters. We are working, as you know, Mr. Speaker, to resist the forces of protectionism wherever they are found. That is why we worked so vigorously for a new round of multilateral trade negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Our free trade agreement with the United States is a major building block in the Government's strategy to strengthen Canada's competitive position in the world and to enhance the prosperity of our people. The free trade agreement will provide greater opportunities for economies of scale in Canadian production and marketing. It will encourage greater productivity and stimulate innovation. It will lead to a more efficient and lower cost Canadian economy.
The economic benefits of the free trade agreement will start to be realized shortly after its implementation on January 1, 1989. Consumer prices will continue to decline, expanding the purchasing power of Canadians. Investment in plant and equipment will expand as Canadian firms move to take advantage of their enhanced access to the huge U.S. market.
The phase-out of tariffs in the free trade agreement will not only mean lower consumer prices, they will give our industries an advantage over the rest of the world in the U.S. market. They will allow integrated North American industries to become more competitive against overseas competition. They will also end a major barrier to value-added processing prior to export, something we sought in the last round of GATT negotiations. The agreement also achieves important new progress in the area of government procurement by expanding the opportunities for suppliers of goods to government markets. The further opening up of government procurement means a new $3 billion market for Canadian business, with the potential for further liberalization in the GATT or future bilateral negotiations.
The Budget-Mr. Daubney
I would like to say a word about productivity and how it relates to the free trade initiatives, to the economic performance of the country and the economic leadership of the Government. As you know, Mr. Speaker, improvements in productivity brought us the surplus which transformed the western world from agrarian to industrial and then to postindustrial society. In our periods of most rapid productivity growth, government services and our personal wealth increased the most rapidly. Since 1973, a period which coincides with the growth in the Canadian deficit from zero to its current levels, Canadian productivity grew very slowly. The result? A sharp jump in unemployment; increased levels of poverty in the country, specifically in the regions; slow growth in personal income, and growing pessimism about our ability to compete with the rest of the world.
If Canada is to increase its national wealth, we need to go beyond our own borders, to sell our services and our products to the rest of the world and to make a profit on the deal. Canadian business cannot, with our small population and fragmented domestic market, grow quickly enough to create the new wealth we need as a nation. Because our markets are small, per capita production in Canada has not matched that in the United States. American industry, of course, can afford to specialize and invest in huge production runs. By the nature of the size of our domestic markets, Canadian productivity begins with a disadvantage, and that is why our output per worker has traditionally been lower than that in the United States.
Can Government help increase productivity? I think the answer to that is yes. It will not do it, however-and I think the record is clear on this-by coddling Canadian industry, by providing it with endless protection against the reality of world competition.
Canadian workers are generally productive, but Canadian managers have tended to be unimaginative and cautious, turning to Government for protection at every ripple in the international economic system. Canadian manufacturing managers in the past have seen threats where they should have seen challenges and opportunities.
There are things the Government can do to improve our economic performance and our chances of creating new wealth. I think the Minister, in his budget speech, spoke about our record of accomplishments to date, a record of which we can be proud. Free trade is part of that record. It is one opportunity, and only an opportunity in my view, not a sure thing, for Canadian industry to improve its productivity. Our productivity is at present 9 per cent behind the American level. If we had unrestricted access to the American market, making use of the same economies of scale which have given them an advantage over us in the past, the best of our companies would be much better off. There is good reason to believe that our productivity and per capita wealth would exceed American levels.

February 22, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Daubney
I want to return briefly to the free trade agreement which is such an integral part of this Government's economic strategy. 1 want to refer in particular to the energy sector where we have secured access for our hydro, uranium, oil and gas exports to the lucrative U.S. market. This is a critical step, as you would know as an Albertan, Mr. Speaker, in ensuring our own energy security. After price, economies of scale made possible by secure access to the U.S. market are the most important factors in allowing us to develop our huge hydro, tar sands and frontier resources. If we do not develop those supplies, we will be the ones who are increasingly reliant on offshore supplies.
In other areas of the agreement we have built on the GATT Standards Code, attacking some of the most devious non-tariff barriers to trade like artificial health standards. We have also created greater certainty for Canadian and U.S. investors. We have retained the right to review significant direct invest proposals. Current restrictions in key sectors remain. The special status of our cultural industries has been entrenched. Perhaps just as important, our own investors will be protected from potential U.S. restrictions. That is clearly important when you consider the extent of our own investment in the U.S. In fact, few Canadians understand that for the past decade we have invested $3 in the U.S. for every $1 invested here by Americans. At the current rate, that means we will soon have as much invested in the U.S. as they have up here, despite the fact they are 10 times our size.
Even more important for future investment patterns is the greater access for Canadian-made goods made possible by the agreement. Increased access for Canadian imports will limit the need for our companies to jump U.S. trade barriers and set up shop in the U.S. We believe it will also allow third country investors to contemplate Canada as the location for their North American facilities.
The economic record of the last three and a half years is one of which we can be proud. The Canadian economy is growing stronger, more dynamic, and better able to compete. In those three and a half years since we set out our agenda for economic renewal, our progress has been dramatic. Over-all, we have done better than any of the other major industrialized nations. We have been number one in economic growth since 1984. We have been number one in employment growth. More than
1,150,000	jobs have been created since we came into office. The great majority of those jobs are full-time in occupations with above average salary levels. The unemployment rate today is the lowest in six years. Economic and employment growth last year was more evenly balanced among the regions. Mortgage rates are three percentage points lower, saving home owners $1,200 a year on a $50,000 mortgage amortized over 25 years. Housing starts have reached a 10-year high. Business is confident. The pace of investment has increased sharply. Consumers are confident. Consumer spending has continued to grow steadily. We have built a solid record of progress, a record of how our policies and initiatives have worked in building the framework for the economic success we now enjoy.
For 1988 the economy is on course for a sixth consecutive year of expansion. The outlook for 1989 is even more encouraging. Canadians have good reason to look forward to the next decade with confidence.

4.	failed to specify a Canadian approach for dealing with the instabilities of the international monetary system."
In amendment to the amendment, Mr. Cassidy, seconded by Mr. Riis, has moved:
That the amendment be amended by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House further condemns the Government for introducing a budget that ignores the real economic needs of the country in which over 1.1 million Canadians are unemployed and eight out of ten provinces and the territories continue to experience employment and income disparities equal to those of the 1981-83 recession;
-for increasing the tax burden of average Canadian families to a level of $ 1,125.00 over the 1984 level through yet another increase in gas taxes;
-for failing to bring fairness to the tax system through the elimination of costly tax breaks and the introduction of a corporate minimum tax that would ensure fair and regular tax payment from those 60,000 profitable corporations that will pay no tax following Conservative tax reform;
-for maintaining a policy of high interest rates begun by previous Liberal governments; and
-for failing to introduce a system of universal child care that would assist average Canadian families and create jobs."
